domains.name: Zero Trust Endpoint Operations
domains.summary: Operating a default-deny endpoint fleet: allowlisting discipline, Ringfencing containment, just-in-time elevation, storage and network control, assume-breach thinking, and the change-control habits that keep security and usability from becoming enemies.
key_points: Default-deny vs default-allow: approve the finite known-good list, not the infinite known-bad list
Ringfencing leashes allowed apps across four dimensions: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Rule strength: certificate over hash over path — never path rules in user-writable locations
Elevation is just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, and logged — never standing admin
Storage by serial, network by destination; assume breach throughout
Change control: scoped fixes, double validation, rollback plans — speed never cancels the process

scenarios.title: The ransomware that wasn’t on any list
scenarios.situation: A brand-new ransomware variant hits a peer company. No vendor has a signature for it yet. Your CISO asks why your endpoints would fare differently — and wants the answer in plain language for the board summary.
scenarios.prompt: What is the core of the answer?
evidence: blocklisting
Default-allow asks: do I recognize this as bad? Unknown code runs until someone proves it malicious — the window every zero-day lives in.
allowlisting
Default-deny asks: is this explicitly trusted? The novel ransomware was never approved, so it never executes — no signature required.
the tradeoff
The cost is operational: every legitimate new app needs an approval path. That is what Learning Mode, the Approval Center, and certificate rules exist to manage.
choices: Our antivirus updates faster than theirs

Default-deny inverts the question from “is this known-bad?” to “is this explicitly trusted?” — the novel ransomware was never approved, so it never runs, with no signature needed; the operational cost is managed through Learning Mode, certificate rules, and the Approval Center
We would be equally exposed; security is mostly luck
Blocklisting is stronger because it only stops confirmed threats
scenarios.why: This is the entire philosophy in one incident: enumerating badness can never be complete, so the model approves known-good instead. Naming the operational cost — and the machinery that pays it — shows you understand this is an engineering tradeoff, not magic, which is what makes the board version credible.
scenarios.hint: Which list is finite: every malicious file that could ever exist, or every application this business needs?

scenarios.title: Word wants to launch PowerShell
scenarios.situation: Unified Audit flags: WINWORD.EXE spawned powershell.exe with an encoded command, then reached out to an external IP. The document came from a vendor email. Word itself is an approved, signed application — no allowlist or signature engine would stop it from launching.
scenarios.prompt: What does this incident teach about application control versus antivirus?
evidence: the bypass
Word is trusted and signed. The attack lives not in WHETHER Word runs, but in WHAT Word was allowed to do once running.
ringfencing dimensions
Four independent leashes: application-to-application interaction, file access, registry access, network access.
living off the land
Attackers prefer trusted binaries precisely because they inherit trust. Containment assumes the app is already compromised.
choices: Remove Word from the allowlist — Office is too dangerous to permit

This is exactly what Ringfencing is for: Word stays approved, but policy denies it from spawning PowerShell, reading the credential store, and reaching unapproved network destinations — containment assumes breach even of trusted apps
Quarantine the endpoint and reinstall Windows; policy cannot help
Add powershell.exe to the blocklist globally
scenarios.why: Application control answers “may it run?”; Ringfencing answers “what may it do once running?” Living-off-the-land attacks exploit the gap between those two questions. Removing Office breaks the business; blocklisting PowerShell globally breaks administration. Containment threads the needle.
scenarios.hint: The malicious thing here is not a file — it is a behavior. Which control governs behavior?

scenarios.title: Payroll is down: the false-positive drill
scenarios.situation: Monday 8:04 a.m.: twelve Finance endpoints block the payroll updater after an overnight policy push. The binary is signed by the real vendor; the hash changed with the new version. This is a version-change false positive, not an attack — but payroll does not care about the distinction.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct change-control response?
evidence: diagnosis
Unified Audit: signed by the known vendor certificate, hash not in catalog — a version-change false positive, not an attack.
narrow fix
A certificate/publisher rule covers the vendor’s future versions; a hash rule would break again at the next update. Scope it to the updater and its child installer.
change control
Emergency change still gets a ticket, a tested scope, a rollout window, and a rollback plan — speed does not cancel the process.
choices: Roll back the entire policy push and leave endpoints unprotected until next week

Confirm the vendor signature in Unified Audit, issue a scoped certificate-based rule for the updater and its child process, deploy, validate the install succeeds AND an unrelated unsigned binary still gets denied, and log the emergency change with a rollback step
Approve the new hash globally for all users permanently
Tell Finance to wait for the next scheduled change window
scenarios.why: Certificate rules survive version churn where hash rules do not; scoping prevents the exception from becoming a hole; and the double validation — the good path works, the bad path stays denied — is what separates a fix from a bypass. Emergency changes follow the process faster, not without it.
scenarios.hint: Fix the narrowest thing that unblocks payroll without unblocking everything else.

scenarios.title: The mystery USB drive
scenarios.situation: A facilities contractor plugs an unrecognized USB drive into a reception PC and a copy dialog opens. Storage Control is in Monitor Only. The drive’s serial is not in the approved-device list, and file operations may already have occurred.
scenarios.prompt: What should the Storage Control posture have been, and what do you do now?
evidence: default posture
Unapproved devices do not connect — allow by serial number, user, file type, and time window, with mandatory encryption or read-only options.
current state
Monitor Only observed but did not block; the copy dialog means file operations may already have happened.
audit trail
Every file copied, moved, or deleted on controlled storage is audited — check what actually happened before deciding the scope of response.
choices: Leave Monitor Only on — blocking USB drives annoys people

Enforce the deny-by-default posture for unknown serials, audit the file operations that already occurred from the logs, contain the reception PC until the drive’s contents are assessed, and approve contractor devices only via time-boxed, read-only, serial-scoped access
Ban all USB devices everywhere permanently
Format the drive and hand it back to the contractor
scenarios.why: Storage Control’s power is granularity: serial-scoped, time-boxed, read-only access instead of a binary allow/ban. But first the audit trail tells you what already happened — respond to the evidence, then tighten the posture so the next unknown drive never mounts.
scenarios.hint: What did Monitor Only buy you, and what would enforcement have bought you?

scenarios.title: The beacon nobody approved
scenarios.situation: A workstation’s approved backup agent starts opening HTTPS connections to an IP in a foreign ASN every 90 seconds. Network Control logs the flows as allowed under a broad “backup application” rule. The agent may be compromised or misconfigured.
evidence: the gap
The rule approved the APPLICATION, not its destinations. Egress allowlisting must scope where an app may talk, not just that it may talk.
assume breach
Treat the flow as hostile until proven otherwise — the agent is a foothold candidate, not a trusted friend.
least privilege
Rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs can pin the agent to the vendor’s known backup endpoints only.
choices: Block all HTTPS from the workstation

Isolate the host, then replace the broad rule with egress allowlisting scoped to the vendor’s known backup destinations (port/IP-scoped, dynamic ACLs), and investigate the beaconing as a potential compromise — approval of the app never implied approval of every destination
Uninstall the backup agent
Ignore it — HTTPS to unknown IPs is normal
scenarios.why: This is Ringfencing’s network dimension applied at the host firewall: least privilege for destinations. A broad application rule recreated the flat-trust problem Zero Trust was hired to kill. Scope the where, investigate the why — and isolate first, because assume-breach means the beacon is guilty until proven innocent.
scenarios.hint: The policy said the app could talk. It never said to whom.

scenarios.title: Assume breach: the admin account audit
scenarios.situation: An access review finds 40 users with standing local-admin rights “from before the rollout,” plus three admin accounts belonging to people who left months ago. No incidents — yet. The CISO wants a remediation plan, not a shrug.
evidence: standing privilege
Every standing admin is pre-staged privilege escalation. Attackers do not hack in; they log in — with the rights you left lying around.
elevation control
Replace standing rights with just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed elevation; auto-remove unused and unauthorized local admin accounts.
monitoring
Every elevated session is logged and audited; elevated processes get ringfenced against application hopping.
choices: Leave them — no incident means no problem

Remove standing local-admin rights, replace with just-in-time per-app elevation for documented needs, purge orphaned accounts, ringfence elevated processes, and keep every elevated session logged and reviewed
Give everyone domain admin so access reviews pass trivially
Delete the admin accounts but keep a shared admin password for emergencies
scenarios.why: Assume breach means designing as if the attacker already has a foothold — and standing admin IS the foothold. The remediation is not just removal but replacement: a usable, audited elevation path, or users will route around you and recreate the risk unofficially.
scenarios.hint: If an attacker phishes one of those 40 users today, what do they inherit?

scenarios.title: The rollout revolt
scenarios.situation: Week one of enforced allowlisting: the helpdesk is drowning, two department heads demand the project be killed, and a VP forwards a complaint thread to the CISO. The policies are technically correct — the deployment around them was not.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right operational response?
evidence: the real failure
Technically correct policy with no communication plan, no staged rollout, and no fast approval path is a deployment failure, not a user failure.
pressure valves
Monitor Only mode for new app classes, Testing Environment pre-approval, and a staffed Approval Center with a published SLA turn blocks into brief pauses.
metrics
Track block rate, approval latency, and repeat requests — you cannot tune what you do not measure.
choices: Push through — security requires suffering
Kill the rollout and go back to antivirus-only

Pause enforcement for the noisiest app classes (Monitor Only), publish the approval SLA, staff the Approval Center through the transition, pre-approve via the Testing Environment, and tune with block-rate and approval-latency metrics — then re-enforce in stages
Exempt executives and department heads from all policies
scenarios.why: Security versus usability is a false choice when the deployment is engineered: staged enforcement, fast approvals, and measured tuning keep the deny-by-default posture while the organization adapts. Exempting leadership just moves the risk onto the most-targeted accounts in the company.
scenarios.hint: The policies are correct — so what part of the rollout was not?

scenarios.title: The 12% that never checks in
scenarios.situation: Monday health review: agent check-in rate is 88% — 30 machines haven't reported in over 14 days. They span departments, include 4 finance workstations, and nobody flagged it because 'the dashboard is usually green.' The assessor asks for your response.
evidence: The finding
12% of the fleet outside policy for 14+ days: unprotected, unmonitored, unpatched-by-policy. The 'green dashboard' was green because nobody looked at this metric.
The risk
4 finance workstations among the 30: the highest-value targets are in the blind spot. Coverage gaps are not uniform risk.
The response

Immediate: investigate the 30 (agent broken? machines decommissioned? users disabling?), prioritize the finance 4, remediate or reimage. Systemic: daily agent-health check with alerting below 99%, and an owner for the metric.
choices: Wait for the next quarterly review; 88% is close enough

Investigate the 30 outliers immediately (prioritizing the 4 finance machines), remediate or reimage, and institute a daily agent-health check with alerting below 99% plus an owner — the gap is both an incident (unprotected machines) and a process failure (unmonitored metric)
Reinstall the agent on all 30 machines today
Exclude the 30 from the health metric so the dashboard is green
scenarios.hint: Eighty-eight percent — is that a passing grade when the missing 12% includes Finance?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it treats the gap as both an immediate incident (unprotected machines, finance prioritized) and a process failure (the metric was unmonitored), and installs the daily check with alerting and ownership. A is wrong: 'close enough' for a security coverage metric ignores that the 12% includes the highest-value targets. C is wrong: mass reinstall without diagnosing WHY they stopped checking in (broken agent? disabled? decommissioned?) repeats the failure. D is wrong: excluding machines from the metric to green the dashboard is the exact dishonesty the scenario is testing.

scenarios.title: The Zero Trust Endpoint Operations Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Zero Trust Endpoint Operations is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Zero Trust Endpoint Operations?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Zero Trust Endpoint Operations issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Zero Trust Endpoint Operations is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Zero Trust Endpoint Operations supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Zero Trust Endpoint Operations failure in Tl Endpoint Ops.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Zero Trust Endpoint Operations
evidence: System Status

scenarios.title: The silent 30%
scenarios.situation: GPO push to 200 machines Friday. Monday: 140 checking in, 60 silent. No install logs (logging wasn't enabled). The desktop team says 'the GPO applied.' The assessor asks for your diagnosis plan.
evidence: What you know
140/200 checking in: the method works for most. 60 silent with no install logs: the failure mode is unknown by design.
The triage
Sample the silent 60: check 5 machines directly — is the agent installed? Is the token present? Can they reach the management plane? The sample diagnoses the population.
The process failure
No install logging turned a diagnosable problem into a guessing game. The immediate fix is diagnosis; the systemic fix is logging on every future push.
choices: Repush the GPO to all 200; the 60 will probably pick it up

Sample 5 silent machines directly (installed? token? reachability?), diagnose the pattern from the sample, fix the population accordingly — and enable install logging on every future push so the next failure is diagnosable
Assume the 60 are decommissioned and ignore them
Manually install on all 60
scenarios.hint: Sixty silent, zero logs. What is the SMALLEST investigation that diagnoses the POPULATION?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it samples instead of guessing (5 machines diagnose 60), fixes by pattern, and repairs the process (logging) that made this a mystery. A is wrong: re-pushing blindly may or may not fix an undiagnosed cause — and teaches nothing. C is wrong: assuming 60 machines are decommissioned without verification is how unprotected machines hide. D is wrong: manual install on 60 without knowing WHY the push failed guarantees the next push fails the same way.

scenarios.title: The macOS surprise
scenarios.situation: Windows deployment went smoothly. macOS rollout: 0 of 15 checking in. The team 'didn't know Macs needed anything special.' Investigation: the agent needs MDM profile approvals (system extension, Full Disk Access) that were never planned. The assessor asks for the recovery.
evidence: The miss
Platform prerequisites treated as a troubleshooting surprise instead of a deployment step. macOS agent deployment IS the MDM approval workflow.
The recovery
Enroll the Macs in the MDM (or approve profiles manually for 15), push/approve the required profiles, then install the agent — in that order. Approvals before install, always.
The lesson
Platform prerequisites belong in the deployment plan's first page, not in the incident review. Windows-first teams must plan macOS (and Linux) as separate workstreams.
choices: Keep reinstalling the agent until it works

Sequence it properly: MDM enrollment/profile approvals FIRST (system extension, Full Disk Access), then agent install — and add platform prerequisites to the deployment plan template so the next platform isn't a surprise
Skip macOS; the Macs can stay unmanaged
Give the Mac users admin and have them approve everything themselves
scenarios.hint: Zero of fifteen. Is this fifteen failures — or one missing prerequisite?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it identifies the single missing prerequisite, sequences the recovery correctly (approvals before install), and fixes the template. A is wrong: reinstalling without the approvals repeats the failure indefinitely. C is wrong: leaving 15 machines unmanaged is the coverage gap the program exists to close. D is wrong: making users approve security profiles themselves is unscalable and insecure.

scenarios.title: The decommissioned ghosts
scenarios.situation: Health review: 25 machines haven't checked in for 60+ days. Investigation: 18 were decommissioned (never removed from the console), 5 are in a storage closet ('spares'), 2 are genuinely broken agents on active machines. The assessor asks what this tells you.
evidence: The breakdown
18 ghosts (asset process failure), 5 closet machines (lifecycle failure), 2 real (agent failure). Three different problems wearing one metric.
What it tells you
The deployment health metric is polluted by asset hygiene: you cannot measure protection while the inventory includes the dead. And the 2 real ones hid among the 23 noise.
The fixes

Asset process: decommissioning removes the console record (tie to the asset system). Closet: spares get agents on reissue, not before. Real: fix the 2 agents. Then the metric measures protection again.
scenarios.prompt: What does this tell you, and what do you fix?
choices: Reinstall agents on all 25

The 25 are three different problems: fix the asset process (decommission removes console records), the spares lifecycle (agents on reissue), and the 2 real agent failures — then the health metric measures protection instead of inventory noise
Delete all 25 from the console
Ignore the ghosts; focus on the 2 real ones
scenarios.hint: Twenty-five non-reporters, three root causes. What happens if you treat them as one problem?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it decomposes the metric into its three causes and fixes each at its root — asset process, lifecycle, and the actual agent failures. A is wrong: reinstalling on decommissioned machines and closet spares is theater. C is wrong: deleting all 25 also deletes the 2 real machines' records — destroying the evidence of the actual problem. D is wrong: ignoring the ghosts leaves the metric permanently polluted, so the NEXT 2 real ones will hide again.

scenarios.title: The remote-user gap
scenarios.situation: Deployment complete: office machines 100%, remote users 62%. The remote 38% 'will install when they're in the office' — some haven't been in for months. Two of them are executives. The assessor asks how you close the gap.
evidence: The reality
'When they're in the office' is not a deployment plan for a remote workforce — it is an indefinite exemption for the hardest-to-reach (and often most-targeted) users.
The mechanism

Remote-capable deployment: MDM/management-tooling push over VPN/internet, or a self-service installer with the token embedded and check-in verification — plus a deadline with consequences (network access requires the agent).
The executives
The two executives get white-glove remote deployment (scheduled, assisted), not an exemption. Most-targeted accounts, least excuse.
scenarios.prompt: How do you close the remote gap?
choices: Wait until they come to the office; it will happen eventually

Deploy remotely-capable methods (MDM/tooling push or token-embedded self-service installer with check-in verification), set a deadline tied to network access, and give the executives white-glove assisted installs — remote users get deployment, not indefinite exemption
Exempt remote users; they are hard to reach
Extend the deadline another quarter
scenarios.hint: 'When they're in the office' — for users who never come in, what does that sentence actually mean?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it provides the actual mechanism (remote-capable push or verified self-service), enforces with a real deadline (network access requires the agent), and handles executives with assistance instead of exemption. A is wrong: 'eventually' is the indefinite exemption restated. C is wrong: exempting remote users — including executives — abandons the most-exposed population. D is wrong: extending the deadline without changing the mechanism just schedules the same failure later.

scenarios.title: The conflicting old agent
scenarios.situation: New agent push fails on 40 machines: the previous vendor's agent is still installed and conflicts (both hook the same subsystems). The old agent's uninstall requires its own console, whose admin left last year. The assessor asks for your path.
evidence: The blocker
Two endpoint agents conflicting: the old one must go before the new one works. The old console's admin is gone — a credential/access recovery problem, not a technical one.
The path

Recover old-console access (vendor support, credential recovery, or the documented break-glass), script the old agent's removal, verify removal, then push the new agent. In that order — removal verified BEFORE new install.
The lesson
Migrations need the old vendor's offboarding in the plan: console access, uninstall method, and conflict testing in the pilot. 'Install the new one' is half a migration plan.
choices: Install the new agent anyway; they can coexist

Recover old-console access, script and verify the old agent's removal, then deploy the new agent — and add vendor offboarding (console access, uninstall method, conflict testing) to the migration template
Leave the 40 on the old agent indefinitely
Manually uninstall on all 40 without the console
scenarios.hint: Two agents, one subsystem, zero coexistence. What has to happen FIRST — and what was missing from the plan?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it sequences correctly (recover access → remove → verify → deploy) and fixes the template (offboarding is part of migration planning). A is wrong: conflicting endpoint agents do not coexist — they fight, and the endpoint loses. C is wrong: 40 machines on a dead vendor's agent is an unprotected, unpatched population. D is wrong: manual uninstall on 40 without the console's method risks partial removals that are worse than the conflict.

scenarios.title: The version-drift discovery
scenarios.situation: Audit: agents range from v4.1 to v4.9 across the fleet. v4.1 lacks the current ringfencing features the policy assumes. Nobody owns agent updates — 'the vendor handles it' (they don't). The assessor asks for the remediation.
evidence: The exposure
Policy assumes features the oldest agents lack: the policy is newer than the fleet. v4.1 machines are policy-noncompliant by version, not by configuration.
The ownership gap
'The vendor handles it' was never verified: no update mechanism, no owner, no monitoring. Drift was inevitable.
The remediation

Immediate: update the laggards (rings, like deployment). Systemic: assign ownership, define the update mechanism (auto vs managed rings), monitor version compliance like check-in compliance — versions are part of health.
choices: The old versions work fine; leave them

Update the laggards in rings, then assign ownership of agent updates, define the update mechanism and cadence, and monitor version compliance as part of daily health — versions are a health metric, not a vendor afterthought
Force-update the entire fleet tonight
Downgrade the policy to v4.1's feature set
scenarios.hint: The policy assumes features the fleet lacks. Is that a policy problem, a fleet problem — or an ownership problem?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it fixes the immediate drift (ringed updates), then the systemic gap (ownership, mechanism, monitoring) — treating versions as a health metric. A is wrong: 'works fine' ignores that the policy's ringfencing assumptions don't hold on v4.1. C is wrong: fleet-wide forced updates tonight is the un-ringed change the whole domain warns against. D is wrong: downgrading the policy to the oldest agent lets drift dictate the security posture.

domains.name: Baseline & Learning Mode
domains.description: Cataloging the fleet's real application footprint before enforcement: window design, uncommon-app adjudication, and the enforcement decision.

scenarios.title: The unmonitored window
scenarios.situation: Learning Mode ran 30 days. On review: the catalog includes 'invoice-decryptor.exe' on 3 endpoints — ransomware from a phishing email that detonated on day 12, was cleaned on day 13, and was never linked to the baseline. The assessor asks for the failure chain.
evidence: Failure 1
Unmonitored window: the day-12 detonation was cataloged as observed behavior and triaged by nobody.
Failure 2
Unreviewed uncommon list: the ransomware's entries sat in the highest-risk list unexamined.
Failure 3
Unlinked incident: the day-13 cleanup never cross-referenced the baseline. The left hand cleaned; the right hand was about to approve.
choices: The antivirus failed to stop the ransomware

Three linked failures: the window was unmonitored (detonation cataloged as known-good), the uncommon list was unreviewed (the entries sat in the riskiest list), and the incident was never linked to the baseline — fix with window monitoring, uncommon adjudication, and incident-to-baseline linkage
The users failed by clicking the phish
Learning Mode is unsafe and should be banned
scenarios.hint: The ransomware is IN the draft baseline. Walk backward: which three gates should have caught it?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it traces the exact cascade and maps each fix to a failure — the complete systemic answer. A is wrong: Learning Mode is DESIGNED to observe; the failure was the missing monitoring and review around it. C is wrong: user-blame ignores the three process failures that weaponized one click into a fleet approval. D is wrong: monitored, reviewed Learning Mode is safe — the concept didn't fail, the controls around it did.

scenarios.title: The 7-day window
scenarios.situation: Leadership demands enforcement in 10 days. The team runs a 7-day Learning Mode window, then enforces fleet-wide. Month-end apps (days 28-31) were never observed. On the 29th, Finance is blocked mid-close. The assessor asks what went wrong.
evidence: The error
A 7-day window cannot catalog a 30-day business cycle. The unobserved month-end apps were never baselined — enforcement blocked them by design.
The deeper error
Schedule pressure overrode evidence: the window was sized to the deadline, not the business calendar.
The recovery
Immediate: scoped temporary allows for the verified close apps. Then: a proper full-cycle window, then re-enforcement. And the lesson: window duration follows the business, not the project plan.
choices: Finance failed to report their apps in time

The window was sized to the deadline instead of the business cycle: month-end apps were never observed, never baselined, and enforcement blocked them by design — recover with scoped temporary allows for verified apps, then run a proper full-cycle window
The team should have worked faster
Finance should be exempt from enforcement
scenarios.hint: How long is the business cycle? How long was the window? Your answer is in the comparison.
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it diagnoses the structural error, recovers narrowly, and re-runs the window properly — plus the meta-lesson about sizing windows to business cycles. A is wrong: blaming Finance reverses the responsibility — window design was the team's job. C is wrong: 'work faster' doesn't change what a 7-day window can observe. D is wrong: exempting Finance is the departmental bypass.

scenarios.title: The bulk-approval proposal
scenarios.situation: 22 uncommon apps. The project lead: 'Just approve them all — we're behind schedule.' The assessor asks for your response.
evidence: What uncommon means
The risk concentration of the baseline: niche tools AND footholds both live here. Highest-value review in the project.
The proposal
Bulk-approving the riskiest 22 entries unverified to protect a date — schedule pressure applied to exactly the wrong list.
The path
Adjudicate each (owner, signer, install date); narrow-scope the verified niche tools; investigate the unknowns. The schedule absorbs days — not skipped verification.
choices: Agree; the schedule is a commitment

Reject bulk approval: adjudicate each of the 22 (owner interview, signer/hash, install-date sanity), scope verified niche tools narrowly, investigate unknowns — the uncommon list is the highest-value review precisely because footholds hide there
Delete all 22 to save time
Approve now, review 'later'
scenarios.hint: Twenty-two apps seen almost nowhere. Rush list — or read list?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it explains WHY the list matters, gives the adjudication method, and prices the schedule honestly. A is wrong: 'probably fine' is the pre-incident sentence. C is wrong: deleting may kill niche business tools — adjudicate, don't nuke. D is wrong: 'review later' after fleet approval is the finding being tested.

scenarios.title: The pruning nobody did
scenarios.situation: Baseline review: 40 applications nobody uses — abandoned trials, games, three versions of the same PDF reader. The team enforced them all 'to keep the schedule.' Six months later, two of the abandoned apps have known vulnerabilities. The assessor asks for the finding.
evidence: The finding
The baseline was enforced, not reviewed: 40 unneeded apps got rules instead of removal tickets. The 'review' was a rubber stamp.
The consequence
Two abandoned apps now carry known vulnerabilities — approved, fleet-wide, unmaintained. The baseline became attack surface.
The fix

Immediate: remove the unneeded apps (tickets, verified). Systemic: the review step must include PRUNING as an explicit gate — 'which apps get removal tickets?' is a review question, not an afterthought.
choices: No finding; approved apps are safe by definition

Finding: the baseline review skipped pruning — 40 unneeded apps were granted rules instead of removal tickets, and two now carry known vulns; remediate by removing the unneeded apps and making pruning an explicit review gate
Uninstall all 40 immediately with no tickets
The vulnerabilities are the vendor's problem
scenarios.hint: Forty apps nobody uses, all approved fleet-wide. What is that — a baseline or an attack surface?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it names the skipped step (pruning), traces the consequence (approved vulns), and makes pruning an explicit gate. A is wrong: 'approved' never meant 'safe' — especially for abandoned software. C is wrong: un-ticketed mass uninstalls break the machines that DO use something. D is wrong: the vendor didn't approve them fleet-wide; the team did.

scenarios.title: The acquired company's baseline
scenarios.situation: You acquire a 50-person firm. Their 'baseline' is the last admin's memory — no catalog, no inventory, 200 path rules, admin departed. The assessor asks for your baselining plan for the acquired fleet.
evidence: The starting point
No trustworthy baseline exists: the 200 path rules are neglect, not policy. Assume the acquired fleet's software state is UNKNOWN.
The plan

Monitor-mode Learning window on the acquired fleet (30 days, covering their business cycle), full uncommon-list adjudication (expect a long list), prune aggressively, then migrate onto the standard policy per the wave plan.
The sequencing
Do NOT merge policies: the acquired fleet gets baselined as a greenfield, then integrated. Merging 200 path rules into the standard policy pollutes it.
choices: Merge their 200 rules into our policy; it's their business software

Greenfield baseline: monitor-mode learning window on the acquired fleet, full uncommon adjudication, aggressive pruning, then migrate onto the standard policy per waves — their rules are neglect, not policy, and merging pollutes the standard
Enforce our policy on them Monday
Leave them on their policy indefinitely
scenarios.hint: Their 'baseline' is 200 path rules and a departed admin's memory. Is that a baseline — or a greenfield?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it treats the acquired fleet as unknown (correct), baselines it properly, and protects the standard policy from pollution. A is wrong: merging 200 unscoped path rules imports the neglect. C is wrong: Monday enforcement on an uninventoried fleet is the guaranteed outage. D is wrong: indefinite separate policy compounds the neglect instead of resolving it.

scenarios.title: The go/no-go with red criteria
scenarios.situation: Wave 1 go-live is Friday. Go/no-go review Thursday: inventory complete, BUT the uncommon list is half-adjudicated, the exception SLA is unpublished, and the rollback was never tested. The project sponsor says 'we're 80% ready — go.' The assessor asks for your call.
evidence: The criteria state
Three red: uncommon half-done (unknown software enforced blind), no published SLA (blocks become outages), untested rollback (the safety net is hypothetical).
'80% ready'
The 20% missing is the risk-bearing 20%: unknown apps, unhandled blocks, untested recovery. Readiness isn't an average.
The call
NO-GO with a dated remediation plan: finish adjudication, publish the SLA, test the rollback — then go. A no-go with a plan is professional; a go on red criteria is scheduled regret.
choices: Go; 80% is passing and the sponsor decides
No-go: three red criteria (uncommon unadjudicated, SLA unpublished, rollback untested) are the risk-bearing items — remediate on a dated plan, then go. A no-go with a plan is the professional outcome
Go, but only for half the wave
Defer the decision to the sponsor
scenarios.hint: Eighty percent ready — but WHICH twenty percent is missing? Does readiness average?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it identifies that the missing 20% is the risk-bearing portion, makes the no-go with a dated plan, and owns the decision. A is wrong: the sponsor's pressure doesn't change the criteria — and '80%' averages away the actual risks. C is wrong: half a wave on red criteria is half a scheduled outage. D is wrong: deferring the technical call to the sponsor abdicates the operator's responsibility.

domains.name: Policy Tuning
domains.description: Keeping policy sharp after enforcement: reading block patterns, tightening scopes, pruning stale rules, and the review cadence.

scenarios.title: The Monday ticket avalanche
scenarios.situation: Every Monday for six weeks: 20+ tickets, same design app, blocked after its weekend auto-update. Each Monday the helpdesk approves the new hash. The assessor asks what the pattern means and what the fix is.
evidence: The pattern
Weekly version churn on a hash rule: the textbook hash-on-churn failure, repeating 6 times because each Monday was treated as a new incident.
The cost
120+ tickets, 6 weeks of helpdesk toil, 6 weeks of Monday-morning blocks for the design team — all for one wrong rule type.
The fix

Replace the hash rule with a scoped certificate/publisher rule for the vendor: survives version churn by design. Then the process fix: weekly-repeating tickets trigger pattern review, not repeat approval.
choices: Keep approving weekly; it's only 20 tickets

The pattern is hash-rule version churn: replace with a scoped certificate rule for the vendor (survives updates), and add the process rule that repeating-weekly tickets trigger pattern review instead of repeat approval
Disable the app's auto-update
Approve the app by path
scenarios.hint: Six Mondays, same app, same block. Is this six incidents — or one rule-type error?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it names the pattern, fixes the cause (not the symptom), and adds the process guardrail. A is wrong: normalizing 120 tickets of toil is operational surrender. C is wrong: disabling updates trades toil for security debt. D is wrong: a path rule for a weekly-updating app is a standing hole.

scenarios.title: The 'temporary' grant, one year later
scenarios.situation: Review finds: 'TEMP — contractor project' publisher grant, fleet-wide, all vendor binaries, created 14 months ago, project ended 11 months ago, no owner, no review date. The assessor asks for findings.
evidence: The findings
Four failures in one grant: temporary without expiry (became permanent), fleet-wide for a project need (unscoped), no owner (unreviewable), no review date (undiscoverable until now).
The exposure
14 months of fleet-wide trust in a vendor's entire signed catalog for a project that ended 11 months ago — the grant outlived its need by nearly a year.
The fix

Immediate: remove or re-scope (is ANY of it still needed? verify first). Systemic: temporary grants get automatic expiry — 'temporary' without a date is permanent, and permanence requires the full rule review.
choices: Leave it; removing things is risky

Four findings in one grant (no expiry, unscoped, no owner, no review date) for a project dead 11 months — remove or re-scope after verifying current need, and make automatic expiry mandatory for temporary grants
Renew it for another year to be safe
Ask around to find the owner
scenarios.hint: Fourteen months old, project dead eleven months ago. What was this grant's ACTUAL lifespan — and what set it?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it enumerates all four failures, verifies before removing (don't break what might still be needed), and fixes the mechanism (automatic expiry). A is wrong: 'risky to remove' preserves an 11-month-dead grant indefinitely. C is wrong: renewing a dead project's grant is the decay, formalized. D is wrong: hunting for an owner of a dead project delays the obvious remediation.

scenarios.title: The tuning that broke payroll
scenarios.situation: A 'small tweak' to a publisher rule — narrowed Friday afternoon, pushed fleet-wide without canary — blocks the payroll updater Monday 8 AM. The assessor asks for the failure chain.
evidence: Failure 1
No canary: the tweak went fleet-wide untested. The canary exists precisely for 'small tweaks.'
Failure 2
Friday-afternoon push: the change landed where no one would see the breakage until Monday — maximum blast radius, minimum observation.
Failure 3
The tweak narrowed a rule the author didn't fully understand (the updater's child chain). Tuning without understanding the grant's full shape.
choices: The payroll vendor's fault for updating

Three failures: no canary on a fleet-wide push, Friday-afternoon timing (breakage invisible until Monday), and narrowing a grant whose full shape wasn't understood — immediate fix via rollback, then the process fix (canary mandatory, no Friday pushes, understand-before-narrow)
Bad luck; tweaks sometimes break things
The rule was too complex; simplify all rules
scenarios.hint: Friday push, no canary, Monday payroll down. Which of those three was the decision — and which were habits?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it separates the three failures cleanly, fixes immediately via rollback, and addresses each with a process rule. A is wrong: blaming the vendor ignores that the tweak broke a working grant. C is wrong: 'bad luck' is the refusal to learn. D is wrong: 'simplify all rules' is a slogan, not a remediation.

scenarios.title: The scope the reorg broke
scenarios.situation: After a reorg, the 'Engineering' group grant covers 120 people — including 60 who moved to other departments. The grant: publisher rule, broad vendor suite, fleet-adjacent scope. The assessor asks what the reorg broke.
evidence: What broke
The WHO axis of the scope: group membership drifted, so the grant's actual coverage doubled beyond its intended population.
The exposure
60 non-engineers hold a broad vendor-suite grant they were never meant to have — scope drift via HR, invisible to security.
The fix

Immediate: re-scope to the actual current need (verify who uses the suite). Systemic: tie scope reviews to identity lifecycle — reorgs, role changes, and departures trigger grant re-verification, not just account changes.
scenarios.prompt: What broke, and what is the systemic fix?
choices: Nothing broke; the grant still works

The reorg broke the grant's WHO axis (60 non-engineers now covered) — re-scope to actual current need, and tie scope reviews to identity lifecycle events (reorgs, role changes, departures) so membership drift triggers re-verification
Delete the Engineering group
Revoke the grant from everyone and start over
scenarios.hint: The grant didn't change. The GROUP did. What process watches the group?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it identifies the drifted axis precisely and connects scope review to identity lifecycle — the systemic fix. A is wrong: 'still works' confuses function with authorization — the wrong 60 people are covered. C is wrong: deleting the group breaks identity management to fix a scope. D is wrong: mass revocation punishes the 60 real engineers for an HR-driven drift.

scenarios.title: The quarterly review that found nothing
scenarios.situation: Quarterly policy review completes: 'no findings, policy is healthy.' But the exception register doubled this quarter, approval turnaround tripled, and two departments run shadow approval processes. The assessor asks what the review missed.
evidence: What the review measured
The rules — and the rules may indeed be fine. The review measured the POLICY and missed the OPERATION.
What it missed
Doubled exceptions (baseline drifting), tripled turnaround (approval operation failing), shadow processes (organization routing around the control) — the program is failing around a healthy policy.
The fix
The quarterly review must cover policy AND operations: rules, scopes, exceptions, queue metrics, and shadow-IT signals. A 'healthy' verdict on a failing program is a review-scope failure.
choices: Nothing; the policy is healthy

The review scoped itself to the rules and missed the operation: doubled exceptions, tripled turnaround, and shadow approvals mean the program is failing around a healthy policy — expand the review to cover operations (exceptions, queue, shadow signals), not just rules
The metrics are wrong
Reviews are pointless; skip them
scenarios.hint: Healthy policy, failing program. What did the review look at — and what didn't it look at?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it diagnoses the review-scope failure precisely and expands the review correctly. A is wrong: it repeats the review's own error — the policy isn't the program. C is wrong: the metrics are the signal; dismissing them is the failure. D is wrong: the answer to a bad review is a better review, not none.

scenarios.title: The vendor-suite sprawl
scenarios.situation: Three years ago: publisher grant for 'Vendor Suite' (3 apps used). Today: the vendor has 14 products, all covered by the same grant; the company uses 4. The assessor asks for the finding.
evidence: The finding
Grant scope drifted via vendor catalog growth: the company approves 14 products' worth of trust while using 4. The grant's meaning changed without anyone deciding.
The exposure
10 unused vendor products — including bundled utilities and trialware — carry fleet trust. The vendor's future acquisitions inherit it too.
The fix
Narrow the publisher grant to the 4 used products (scoped by product/filename), review vendor-catalog changes annually, and treat 'vendor added products' as a scope-review trigger.
choices: No finding; it's the same trusted vendor

Finding: the grant's coverage tripled via vendor catalog growth while usage stayed at 4 products — narrow to the used products, review vendor-catalog changes annually, and treat catalog growth as a scope-review trigger
Remove the vendor entirely
Trust the vendor's judgment on their products
scenarios.hint: Three apps then, fourteen now, four used. What changed — the trust, or the catalog?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it identifies catalog-driven scope drift, narrows precisely, and creates the ongoing trigger. A is wrong: 'same vendor' ignores that the grant's coverage tripled without a decision. C is wrong: removing a needed vendor over a scoping issue is disproportionate. D is wrong: the vendor's product strategy is not your risk decision.

domains.name: Override Handling
domains.description: The pressure valve of default-deny: time-boxed, scoped, ticketed overrides that relieve urgency without becoming permanent holes.

scenarios.title: The 4 PM 'just this once'
scenarios.situation: 4:00 PM Friday: a developer needs an unsigned internal tool approved 'just this once' for a weekend deployment. The tool is built in-house, no signer, hash unknown to the catalog. 'The pipeline is down, this is the only build.' The assessor asks for your call.
evidence: The request
Unsigned + unknown + 'just this once' + pipeline-down story: every element argues for verification, none for trust.
The tree
UNKNOWN + URGENT → sandbox first, override never. The pipeline claim is verifiable (check the pipeline); the binary is detonatable (minutes).
The helpful path

'Bring me the pipeline build OR let me detonate this one now — if the pipeline is truly down and the sandbox is clean, we discuss a narrow time-box. But 'just this once' for an unknown is not a thing.'
choices: Approve it; the weekend deployment matters
Deny the override: unknowns don't get overridden — verify the pipeline claim and offer immediate sandbox detonation; a narrow time-box is discussable only AFTER evidence, never before
Approve it for the weekend only
Tell them to wait until Monday
scenarios.hint: 'Just this once' for an unknown binary. What does the tree say — and what can you verify in the next ten minutes?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it holds the tree's red line (unknowns never get overridden), verifies the verifiable (pipeline status), and offers the fast evidence path (sandbox now) — firm on standard, fast on help. A is wrong: the deployment's importance doesn't manufacture trust signals. C is wrong: a weekend-bounded unknown is still an approved unknown. D is wrong: 'wait until Monday' abandons the developer when a ten-minute verification path exists.

scenarios.title: The VP's borrowed authority
scenarios.situation: The VP of Sales emails: 'Approve design-tool.exe for my team immediately — I take responsibility.' The binary: unsigned, first-seen, no sandbox result. The assessor tests rank pressure.
evidence: The evidence
Unsigned, first-seen, no sandbox: zero trust signals. 'I take responsibility' is not a trust signal — it is a pressure signal.
The principle
Authority buys speed, not a lower bar: the VP's request gets the fastest COMPLIANT path (immediate sandbox, expedited review), never a different standard.
The response

'I'll expedite this personally — sandboxing now, decision in 30 minutes. I can't approve an unknown unsigned binary on authority alone; here's what I need to say yes.' Rank gets responsiveness; evidence still decides.
choices: Approve it; the VP takes responsibility

Expedite compliantly: immediate sandbox detonation and a 30-minute decision commitment — the VP gets speed and transparency, but the evidence standard doesn't move for rank; 'I take responsibility' is pressure, not verification
Refuse and report the VP for pressuring security
Ignore the email until the sandbox is done
scenarios.hint: 'I take responsibility' — for WHAT, exactly? Does it verify the binary?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it converts rank pressure into speed (the legitimate response to authority) while holding the standard immovably — and communicates the boundary professionally. A is wrong: responsibility-taking doesn't detonate binaries or verify signers. C is wrong: escalating against the VP for a routine pressure attempt burns the relationship; the professional answer handles it. D is wrong: silence to a VP is not a strategy — communicate the expedited path.

scenarios.title: The third override for the same app
scenarios.situation: Same CAD plugin, third month in a row: JIT override for its monthly update, 40 machines, properly ticketed each time. The assessor asks what the pattern means.
evidence: The pattern
Three identical overrides: the textbook 'rule request in an override costume.' The need is proven durable and predictable.
What it means
The override path is being used as a slow approval queue — the valve has become the process, which means the process is missing.
The fix

Convert: package the update (deploy via management tooling) or write the proper certificate rule for the vendor's updater. Then the rule: third identical override triggers mandatory conversion review.
scenarios.prompt: What does the pattern mean, and what do you do?
choices: Keep overriding; the process works

The third identical override is a conversion signal: package the update or write the proper rule, and add the process trigger (3rd identical override → mandatory conversion review) — the valve must not become the queue
Deny the fourth override to force the issue
Grant a permanent override
scenarios.hint: Three months, same app, same override. At what point does 'temporary' become a lie?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it reads the pattern correctly, converts structurally (packaging or proper rule), and installs the process trigger. A is wrong: 'works' at 40 tickets/month is expensive toil normalized. C is wrong: denying to 'force the issue' punishes users for a process gap. D is wrong: a permanent override is the hole the expiry mechanism exists to prevent.

scenarios.title: The expired-but-active grants
scenarios.situation: Quarterly audit: 12 overrides past expiry still active. The expiry mechanism 'was never configured' — the team tracked expiries in a spreadsheet nobody opened. The assessor asks for the severity and fix.
evidence: The severity
CRITICAL: 12 unexpired-by-design grants active past their authorized window — the temporary control failed open, silently, for an unknown duration.
The root cause
Manual expiry (spreadsheet) for a control that requires automatic enforcement. The mechanism was hope.
The fix

Immediate: review or revoke all 12 (verify current need). Systemic: configure automatic expiry, alert on expired-but-active, and treat the spreadsheet era as the lesson — manual tracking is not a control.
choices: Low; the overrides were all legitimate when granted

Critical: 12 grants active past authorization because expiry was manual (a spreadsheet) — immediately review/revoke all 12, configure automatic expiry with alerting on expired-but-active, and record the lesson that manual tracking is not a control
Delete the spreadsheet
Extend all 12 by 90 days and configure expiry later
scenarios.hint: Twelve grants, past expiry, still active. What failed — the grants, or the mechanism?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it rates the severity correctly (failed-open temporary controls), fixes the instances, and repairs the mechanism (automatic expiry + alerting). A is wrong: 'legitimate when granted' is irrelevant — authorization expired. C is wrong: deleting the spreadsheet deletes the only record of what needs review. D is wrong: extending without review blesses 12 unexamined grants for 90 more days.

scenarios.title: The manufactured urgency
scenarios.situation: A user demands an immediate override: 'client demo in 20 minutes, I need this installer NOW.' The binary: signed by a known vendor, hash matches the published value, but it's not in the allowlist. The assessor asks: override or queue?
evidence: The evidence
Signed by known vendor + hash matches published: the trust signals are STRONG. This is known-good blocked by a rule gap, not an unknown.
The urgency
20-minute demo: verifiable (calendar invite?), real, and short. The urgency claim is checkable.
The tree
KNOWN-GOOD + URGENT + RULE GAP → override: narrow (this binary, this user), brief (24h), ticketed — plus the follow-up: write the proper rule so the next demo doesn't need an override.
choices: Queue; 20 minutes isn't enough time to do it right

Override narrowly: the trust signals are strong (signed, hash-verified) and the urgency is verifiable — grant this binary for this user for 24h with a ticket, then write the proper rule so it never needs an override again
Deny; demos aren't emergencies
Approve permanently to avoid repeat demos
scenarios.hint: Strong trust signals, verifiable urgency, 20 minutes. What does the tree say — and what happens AFTER the demo?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it applies the tree correctly (known-good + urgent + rule gap = override), keeps it narrow and brief, and converts the lesson into the proper rule. A is wrong: 20 minutes is plenty for a verified narrow grant — the queue is for routine, not for this. C is wrong: 'demos aren't emergencies' dismisses a verifiable business need the tree explicitly covers. D is wrong: permanent for a 20-minute need is the scope failure the domain warns against.

scenarios.title: The odd-hour override pattern
scenarios.situation: Override log review: one service account requested 8 overrides in 3 weeks, all between 1-3 AM, all for unsigned binaries, all 'urgent.' Each was approved by the same junior analyst. The assessor asks what you see.
evidence: The pattern
Odd hours + service account + unsigned binaries + 'urgent' + single approver: five anomaly signals converging on the override valve — the pressure valve under targeted use.
What it could be
Compromised service account, malicious insider, or (least likely) a genuinely odd-but-legitimate workflow. The pattern demands investigation, not assumption.
The response

Immediate: freeze the valve for that account (no more overrides pending review), investigate (account activity, binary analysis, approver interview). Systemic: alert on override anomalies (hour, frequency, signer state), require senior approval for unsigned overrides.
scenarios.prompt: What do you see, and what do you do?
choices: A busy service account; approve faster to reduce their pain

An anomaly pattern on the override valve: freeze further overrides for the account pending investigation (account, binaries, approver), and add systemic guards — anomaly alerting on overrides and senior approval for unsigned-binary overrides
Reprimand the junior analyst
Disable the service account immediately
scenarios.hint: Eight overrides, 1-3 AM, unsigned binaries, one approver. How many anomaly signals — and what is being targeted?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it counts the converging signals, freezes the valve (not the business) pending investigation, and builds the systemic guards. A is wrong: 'busy account' ignores five converging anomalies — that read is how intrusions persist. C is wrong: the analyst followed (bad) process; the finding is the process (no anomaly alerting, junior approving unsigned). D is wrong: immediate disable before investigation may destroy evidence and disrupts whatever legitimate function exists — freeze the valve, investigate, then decide.

domains.name: Update Rings
domains.description: Rolling out agent and policy updates safely: ring sequencing, canary metrics, pause criteria, and the rollback discipline.

scenarios.title: The fleet-wide agent update
scenarios.situation: New agent version Friday 5 PM: pushed fleet-wide, no rings, no canary. Monday: 40 machines bluescreen on boot, 200 users idle, the helpdesk is drowning. The assessor asks for the failure chain.
evidence: Failure 1
No rings: the entire fleet took the update simultaneously — maximum blast radius by design.
Failure 2
No canary: nothing measured the update's effect before it was everywhere. The 40 bluescreens were discovered by users, not metrics.
Failure 3
Friday 5 PM: the push landed where no one would see breakage for 60 hours — and the rollback (untested) is now being attempted under fire.
choices: The vendor shipped a bad agent; not our fault

Three failures: fleet-wide push with no rings (maximum blast radius), no canary metrics (breakage discovered by users), Friday-evening timing with an untested rollback — immediate: execute/test rollback on affected rings; systemic: ringed updates with canary cards become mandatory
Bad luck with the vendor
Reinstall Windows on the 40 machines
scenarios.hint: Friday 5 PM, no rings, no canary, untested rollback. Which of those was the DECISION?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it separates the three process failures from the vendor's bad build, acts immediately (rollback), and makes rings mandatory. A is wrong: the vendor's bad build explains 40 bluescreens; YOUR process explains why all 40 happened simultaneously with no warning. C is wrong: 'bad luck' is the refusal to learn. D is wrong: reinstalling Windows treats a deployment failure as 40 individual mysteries.

scenarios.title: The ring-2 pause
scenarios.situation: Agent update rollout: ring 0 clean, ring 1 clean, ring 2 (30% of fleet) shows check-in drop from 99% to 94% at hour 30 of the soak. Pause criteria said 'pause at -3%.' The project lead wants to continue: 'it's probably just laptops sleeping.' The assessor asks for your call.
evidence: The data
-5% check-in vs a -3% pause trigger: the pre-committed criterion FIRED. The criterion was written calmly, in advance, precisely for this moment.
The story
'Probably laptops sleeping' is a hypothesis offered to override a measurement. It might even be true — but the criterion doesn't care about the story; it cares about the number.
The call

PAUSE per the pre-commitment. Then investigate (are they sleeping laptops? check the device types) — paused, not rolled back. If the investigation clears it, resume with the finding documented. The criterion earned its authority by being pre-written.
choices: Continue; it's probably just sleeping laptops
Pause per the pre-committed criterion, then investigate the drop (device types, patterns) while held — resume if cleared, rollback if not. Pre-written criteria override 2 AM hypotheses
Roll back the entire rollout immediately
Ignore the criterion; it was too strict
scenarios.hint: The criterion fired. The story says 'probably fine.' Which one did you write in advance — and why?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it honors the pre-commitment (the entire point of writing criteria calmly in advance), pauses rather than panics (investigate while held), and keeps both paths open. A is wrong: overriding a fired criterion with an uninvestigated hypothesis is exactly what pre-commitment prevents. C is wrong: full rollback for a -5% signal skips the investigation the pause exists to perform. D is wrong: 'too strict' is a conclusion you reach AFTER investigating, not during.

scenarios.title: The bundled update
scenarios.situation: Change window: new agent version AND a major policy revision, pushed together 'to save a window.' Monday: block rate tripled AND 15% of agents won't check in. The team argues about which change caused which symptom. The assessor asks for the finding.
evidence: The finding

Bundled changes with unattributable failures: the block spike could be the policy, the check-in drop could be the agent — or each could be causing the other's symptom. Two changes, one window, zero attribution.
The cost
The team now debugs two hypotheses simultaneously, rollback is ambiguous (which do you revert?), and the window 'saved' is spent twice over in investigation.
The fix now
Roll back BOTH (restore known-good state), then re-apply separately with canary cards — agent first, policy second. The rule going forward: one change per window.
choices: Debug both simultaneously; smart teams can handle it

Finding: bundled agent+policy changes produced unattributable failures — roll back both to known-good, then re-apply separately (agent first, policy second) with canary cards; rule going forward is one change per window
Roll back only the policy; the agent is probably fine
Keep both and tune around the issues
scenarios.hint: Two changes, two symptoms, zero attribution. What does the rollback target — and what rule prevents the next one?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it names the attribution failure as THE finding, restores known-good cleanly (both, not guessed), and sequences the re-application correctly. A is wrong: 'smart teams' still can't attribute confounded changes — the methodology is broken, not the team. C is wrong: 'probably fine' is a guess; the bundling destroyed the evidence needed to know. D is wrong: tuning around confounded failures bakes in whatever the real causes were.

scenarios.title: The emergency agent patch
scenarios.situation: Critical vulnerability in the agent itself: vendor ships an emergency patch, 'deploy immediately.' 500 endpoints. The assessor asks how 'immediately' works with rings.
evidence: The tension
Real: the vulnerable agent is the attack surface. Also real: an un-ringed emergency patch can manufacture the outage the vulnerability only threatened.
Compressed rings

Ring 0 (IT, 2h soak, rollback tested) → ring 1 (10%, 4h) → ring 2 (50%, 8h) → ring 3 (fleet). Same metrics, same pause criteria, compressed timeline — 'immediately' means hours with gates, not minutes without.
The communication
'Emergency patch deploying in compressed rings; ring 0 clean, proceeding' — stakeholders hear speed WITH control, which is what justifies the urgency.
choices: Push fleet-wide now; the vulnerability is critical

Compressed rings with the same metrics and pause criteria: ring 0 in hours (rollback tested there), then expanding — emergency shortens the soak, never blinds the rollout; communicate the ring progress as it happens
Wait for the normal ring schedule; process is process
Patch only the internet-facing machines
scenarios.hint: Critical vuln, 500 endpoints. Does 'emergency' mean 'no rings' — or 'faster rings'?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it preserves the safety mechanism at emergency speed — compressed but complete rings, tested rollback, communicated progress. A is wrong: the vulnerability is critical, but an un-ringed patch risks converting a vulnerability into an outage. C is wrong: the normal schedule ignores the vulnerability's urgency — the process has an emergency path for exactly this. D is wrong: 'internet-facing' misunderstands the agent's exposure — the vulnerable agent is everywhere.

scenarios.title: The soak that caught it
scenarios.situation: Policy update: ring 0 (IT) shows nothing for 20 hours. Hour 22: block rate triples — the new ringfence baseline breaks the IT team's own admin tooling, which runs a weekly job Sunday night. The assessor asks what the soak proved.
evidence: What the soak caught
A time-delayed breakage: the 20 quiet hours weren't 'fine,' they were 'the trigger hadn't fired yet.' The weekly job was the trigger; the soak outlasted the quiet period.
What a shorter soak would have done
A 12-hour soak would have cleared ring 0, and the breakage would have hit ring 1's Sunday night — 10x the blast radius. The soak duration was the control.
The lesson

Soak durations must cover the target population's CYCLES (weekly jobs, month-end, backups) — not just wall-clock time. And: the team's OWN tooling breaking in ring 0 is the ideal catch — contained, understood, fixed before it mattered.
choices: The policy update is bad and should be scrapped

The 22-hour soak caught a cycle-delayed breakage (the weekly Sunday job) that a shorter soak would have missed — soaks must cover business cycles, not just hours; ring 0 catching it on the team's own tooling is the mechanism working exactly as designed
Ring 0 is too small to be useful
The admin tooling should be exempt
scenarios.hint: Twenty quiet hours, then the weekly job fired. What was the quiet — safety, or just waiting?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it reads the timing correctly (cycle-delayed, not absent), extracts the soak-design lesson (cover cycles), and celebrates the catch. A is wrong: the update isn't 'bad' — it needs a scoped exception for the admin tooling, which ring 0 revealed cheaply. C is wrong: ring 0's smallness is WHY the catch was cheap. D is wrong: exempting admin tooling from ringfencing creates the standing hole; scope the exception properly.

scenarios.title: The rollback that wasn't tested
scenarios.situation: Ring 2 shows critical breakage. The runbook says 'roll back.' The rollback fails: the previous agent version's installer was archived offsite, the policy backup is 3 versions old, and nobody has ever run the rollback procedure. The assessor asks for the finding.
evidence: The finding
The rollback was a document, not a capability: untested procedure, missing artifacts (installer archived, stale policy backup). 'We can roll back' was fiction.
The current crisis
Ring 2 is broken with no working revert path: the team now forward-fixes under fire — the most expensive possible position, manufactured by the untested runbook.
The systemic fix

Rollbacks are tested in ring 0 of EVERY rollout (actually execute the revert on the lab machines), artifacts are staged before the rollout (installers local, policy versioned), and the runbook lists the rollback's dependencies. A rollback is a tested capability or it is a hope.
choices: Bad luck; rollbacks usually work

Finding: the rollback was an untested document — missing artifacts and a never-executed procedure meant 'we can roll back' was fiction; systemic fix is testing the rollback in ring 0 of every rollout with staged artifacts, making rollback a capability instead of a hope
Forward-fix faster next time
Blame the runbook author
scenarios.hint: 'We can roll back' — when was that sentence last TESTED? What is an untested rollback?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it names the fiction precisely, handles the current crisis honestly (forward-fix under fire is the price), and makes rollback-testing part of every rollout's ring 0. A is wrong: untested rollbacks fail routinely — this is normal, not luck. C is wrong: 'forward-fix faster' normalizes the missing safety net instead of building it. D is wrong: the author wrote what the process asked for; the process never required testing.

domains.name: macOS Agents
domains.description: Endpoint protection on macOS: MDM approvals, system extensions, Full Disk Access, and the platform differences that surprise Windows-first teams.

scenarios.title: The blind fleet
scenarios.situation: 15 Macs 'deployed' — all checking in, all green. Audit: zero blocks in 30 days, and a known-test unsigned binary executed cleanly on 3 sampled machines. The assessor asks what 'green' means here.
evidence: The finding
Checking in is not protecting: the agents lack Full Disk Access (never approved), so they're blind — the 'green' dashboard measures reporting, not capability.
The test
The unsigned binary executing cleanly is the proof: a default-deny agent that allows unknown execution is not enforcing. Capability test beats dashboard color.
The fix

Push the FDA/system-extension profiles via MDM, verify capability per machine (not just check-in), re-run the execution test, and add capability verification to the deployment checklist — green must mean capable.
scenarios.prompt: What does 'green' mean, and what do you do?
choices: The Macs are protected; zero blocks means zero threats

'Green' meant reporting, not protecting: the agents lack Full Disk Access and are blind (proven by the clean execution of an unsigned test binary) — push the approval profiles, verify capability per machine, re-test execution, and make capability verification part of deployment
Reinstall all 15 agents
The test binary must have been signed
scenarios.hint: Zero blocks in 30 days, unsigned binary runs clean. Is that a quiet fleet — or a blind one?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it distinguishes reporting from capability, uses the execution test as proof, and fixes both the instances and the checklist. A is wrong: 'zero threats' is the dangerous read — the test proved non-enforcement. C is wrong: reinstalling without the approvals reproduces the blindness. D is wrong: the binary was known-unsigned; the hypothesis dodges the finding.

scenarios.title: Gatekeeper vs allowlist: who denied it?
scenarios.situation: User report: 'my app won't open.' The app is allowlisted (hash approved). Console shows no allowlist deny — but macOS shows 'cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified.' The helpdesk wants to 'fix the allowlist.' The assessor asks for the triage.
evidence: The layers
Gatekeeper (Apple's notarization/quarantine gate) sits UNDER the allowlist. The message 'developer cannot be verified' is Gatekeeper's, not the agent's.
The triage

No allowlist deny in the console = the allowlist never saw it. The decision happened at the Apple layer — the fix is notarization/quarantine handling (vendor's signature, quarantine attribute), not an allowlist change.
The lesson
Know which layer decided before 'fixing' anything: changing allowlist rules for a Gatekeeper decision is tuning the wrong control — and the console's silence was the clue.
choices: Fix the allowlist; the hash must be wrong
Gatekeeper denied it (Apple's message, no allowlist deny in console) — the fix is at the Apple layer (notarization/quarantine), not the allowlist; the console's silence was the diagnostic clue
Disable Gatekeeper on the machine
Re-approve the hash
scenarios.hint: No deny in YOUR console, but the app won't open. Which layer decided — and what was the clue?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it reads the layer correctly (message + console silence = Gatekeeper), fixes at the right layer, and extracts the triage lesson. A is wrong: the hash is fine; the allowlist never decided. C is wrong: disabling Gatekeeper fleet-wide for one app's notarization issue is the sledgehammer. D is wrong: re-approving a correct hash changes nothing.

scenarios.title: The OS upgrade avalanche
scenarios.situation: macOS major upgrade weekend: Monday brings 80 tickets — Apple system apps and vendor tools blocked across the Mac fleet. Hashes changed with the OS; the policy wasn't prepped. The assessor asks for the postmortem.
evidence: The cause
OS upgrade as unplanned policy event: hundreds of hashes changed, no pre-approval, Monday discovered it. Hash-churn at OS scale.
The prevention
OS upgrades are policy events: pre-approve via Apple/developer identity rules (survive the churn), pilot the upgrade on IT Macs with the new policy, communicate the window.
Now

Immediate: Apple-identity rules for the system components (not per-hash whack-a-mole), expedited approvals for the vendor tools. Then: the OS-upgrade policy checklist, so the next major version is a planned event.
choices: Apple's fault for changing hashes

The OS upgrade was an unplanned policy event: fix now with Apple-identity rules (not per-hash), expedite vendor tool approvals, and create the OS-upgrade policy checklist (pre-approval, pilot, comms) so the next major version is planned
Block OS upgrades permanently
Approve every blocked hash individually
scenarios.hint: Eighty tickets, one weekend, hundreds of changed hashes. What kind of event was the upgrade — and what should it have been?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it treats the upgrade as the policy event it is, fixes with identity rules (the churn-proof answer), and creates the checklist. A is wrong: Apple changing hashes on a major upgrade is expected behavior — the planning failure was yours. C is wrong: blocking OS upgrades trades policy convenience for security debt. D is wrong: per-hash approval of OS components is the whack-a-mole the identity rules replace.

scenarios.title: The manual-approval mess
scenarios.situation: No MDM for the Macs ('we'll get to it'). Result: 15 users each approved different things in System Settings — 4 granted FDA, 6 granted the system extension only, 5 granted nothing. Capability is random. The assessor asks for the structural fix.
evidence: The state
Capability by user whim: 4 capable, 6 partial, 5 blind. The fleet's protection is a random variable.
The cause
Manual approvals don't scale and don't standardize: every user is a separate deployment decision, and users decide based on confusion.
The structural fix

MDM enrollment + pushed approval profiles: the approvals become deterministic, verifiable, and auditable. 'We'll get to it' is the finding — MDM is the macOS deployment prerequisite, not a future project.
choices: Send better instructions so users approve correctly

The fleet's capability is random because approvals are manual — the structural fix is MDM enrollment with pushed approval profiles (deterministic, verifiable, auditable); manual approval is the finding, not the process
Accept the 4 capable ones as good enough
Remote into each Mac and click approve for them
scenarios.hint: Four capable, six partial, five blind. Is that a deployment — or fifteen improvisations?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it names the randomness as the finding and prescribes the structural fix (MDM profiles). A is wrong: better instructions don't fix a process that depends on 15 confused users. C is wrong: 4 of 15 capable is not a deployment outcome. D is wrong: remote-clicking 15 machines is manual approval with extra steps — unscalable and unauditable.

scenarios.title: The osascript anomaly
scenarios.situation: Audit: a Mac's approved reporting tool spawned osascript with an encoded command at 2 AM, no user logged on. The app-to-app leash allowed 'reporting tool children' broadly. The assessor asks for the read.
evidence: The signals
2 AM + no user + osascript (macOS's built-in automation/LOLBin) + encoded command + broad child allowance: the macOS-shaped living-off-the-land pattern.
The policy gap
'Reporting tool children: allow' is the over-broad leash — it permitted any child, including osascript with encoded input, at any hour.
The response
Isolate and investigate (the 2 AM no-user encoded execution is incident-grade until proven otherwise), then narrow the leash to the tool's actual needed children (pinned, not 'children').
choices: The reporting tool needs osascript; allow it

Incident-grade until proven otherwise: isolate, investigate the 2 AM no-user encoded osascript execution, and narrow the app-to-app leash from 'children: allow' to the tool's actual pinned children — the broad leash is the policy gap
Block osascript system-wide
Ignore it; reporting tools run at night
scenarios.hint: Encoded osascript, 2 AM, no user, broad child leash. Which of those is normal?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it treats the pattern as incident-grade (correct for the signal cluster), investigates before concluding, and fixes the leash precisely. A is wrong: 'needs osascript' doesn't cover 2 AM encoded execution with no user — and the leash was 'children,' not 'osascript for the report.' C is wrong: system-wide osascript block breaks legitimate automation to fix one leash. D is wrong: 'runs at night' doesn't explain encoded commands with no user.

scenarios.title: The /Applications vs ~/Downloads split
scenarios.situation: Policy review: the macOS allowlist uses path rules — /Applications/* allowed, ~/Downloads/* denied. A user installs a vendor tool to ~/Applications (user-writable) to 'avoid the admin prompt.' It runs. The assessor asks for the finding.
evidence: The finding
The policy's path model has a hole: ~/Applications is user-writable and unlisted — the user's workaround runs entirely outside the path policy.
The pattern
The classic user-writable path hole, macOS-flavored: the policy covered /Applications and ~/Downloads but not the third writable location. Attackers (and users) read policies too.
The fix

Cover ~/Applications explicitly (deny, or hash/identity rules for needed tools), and address the root: the 'admin prompt avoidance' signals the approval path is slower than the workaround — fix the path rules AND the approval speed.
choices: The user violated policy; punish them

Finding: ~/Applications is a user-writable path outside the policy's model — cover it explicitly (deny or identity/hash rules), and fix the approval-path speed that made the workaround attractive; the workaround is also a usability signal
Allow ~/Applications too; users need flexibility
The path policy is fine; this is a one-off
scenarios.hint: Three writable locations, two covered. What is the third — and why did the user go there?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it finds the actual hole, fixes it explicitly, and reads the workaround as the usability signal it is. A is wrong: punishment without fixing the hole or the slow approvals guarantees the next workaround. C is wrong: allowing the writable location blesses the hole. D is wrong: 'one-off' ignores that the policy model itself missed a standard macOS path.

domains.name: Linux Agents
domains.description: Endpoint protection on Linux: diverse distros, package-manager deployment, server-vs-workstation policy, and the CLI-native triage.

scenarios.title: The 'blocked' that wasn't yours
scenarios.situation: Dev workstation: 'my build tool is blocked.' Your console shows NO deny for the binary. The system log shows an SELinux denial for the same path at the same timestamp. The dev wants 'the allowlist fixed.' The assessor asks for the triage.
evidence: The decider
SELinux denied it (its audit log names it); your console's silence confirms your policy never saw it. Two MAC systems, one decider.
The triage
