Fix at the SELinux layer (policy module, context label) — not your allowlist. Changing your rules for another control's decision is tuning the wrong system.
The lesson
On Linux, always identify the decider: your agent's log, SELinux/AppArmor's log, or the application's own error. The silent console was the clue — again.
scenarios.prompt: Who denied it, and where is the fix?
choices: Fix the allowlist; add the binary
SELinux denied it (its audit names it; your console is silent) — fix at the SELinux layer (context/policy module), not the allowlist; the silent console was the diagnostic clue
Disable SELinux; it conflicts with the agent
The build tool is incompatible; replace it
scenarios.hint: Your console is silent but the tool is blocked. How many access-control layers does this box have — and which one spoke?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it identifies the decider correctly via the two logs, fixes at the right layer, and extracts the triage lesson. A is wrong: the allowlist never decided; changing it is tuning the wrong control. C is wrong: disabling SELinux removes a security layer to dodge a labeling fix. D is wrong: replacing the toolchain over a context label is the sledgehammer.

scenarios.title: The /tmp execution
scenarios.situation: Incident review: a compromised web app dropped a payload to /tmp and executed it. The allowlist had no rule covering /tmp execution — it 'wasn't in the inventory.' The assessor asks for the finding.
evidence: The finding

/tmp (and /dev/shm) are executable-danger zones on Linux: world-writable, standard payload drop points. The policy's path model ignored them — the inventory covered /usr and /opt but not the attacker's favorite directories.
The fix

Explicit deny-execution policy for /tmp and /dev/shm (noexec mounts where the workflow allows, explicit deny rules where it doesn't), and the inventory must include the danger zones — 'not in the inventory' is the finding, not the excuse.
The upstream
The web app compromise is the incident; the /tmp execution is the control gap it exploited. Fix both: the app AND the path model.
choices: The web app vendor's fault

Finding: the path model ignored Linux's executable-danger zones (/tmp, /dev/shm) — the payload ran where the inventory never looked; fix with explicit noexec/deny for those paths and add them to the inventory model, plus remediate the web app compromise itself
Block all of /tmp; nothing needs it
The allowlist can't cover everything
scenarios.hint: World-writable, standard drop point, unlisted in the inventory. What is /tmp — to you, and to the attacker?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it names the path-model gap precisely, fixes it at both layers (mount/policy + inventory), and doesn't drop the upstream incident. A is wrong: the vendor didn't choose your path model. C is wrong: /tmp has legitimate uses; noexec/deny-execution is the scoped answer, not deletion. D is wrong: 'can't cover everything' surrenders the exact directories attackers use most.

scenarios.title: The container escape attempt
scenarios.situation: Runtime alert: a container tried to mount the host's /etc and spawn a host-networked shell. The container runtime policy denied both. The assessor asks: what does this test, and what's next?
evidence: What was tested
The container runtime's leashes (mount scope, network scope, spawn scope): the escape attempt hit all three, all three held. Defense in depth at the runtime layer.
What it means
Something inside the container is hostile or compromised: the escape attempt is a detection, not a closed ticket. The container is the patient.
What's next

Isolate the host, investigate the container image (which image? whose? when pulled?), hunt for the same image elsewhere, verify no escape succeeded via sibling checks — then fix the supply chain (image provenance).
scenarios.prompt: What was tested, and what's next?
choices: The runtime policy works; close the ticket

The three runtime leashes held against a real escape attempt — treat it as a detection: isolate the host, investigate the image (provenance, pull history), hunt laterally for the same image, verify no escape succeeded, then fix the image supply chain
Delete the container
Restart the runtime
scenarios.hint: Three denies, one container, escape attempted. Is the story 'policy works' — or 'intrusion attempted'?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it treats the denies as detections of a hostile container, runs the full response (isolate, image investigation, lateral hunt, verification), and fixes the supply chain. A is wrong: 'works, closed' ignores the hostile content inside the container. C is wrong: deleting the container destroys the evidence. D is wrong: restarting the runtime addresses nothing about the image or the hunt.

scenarios.title: The distro-upgrade Monday
scenarios.situation: Fleet Ubuntu LTS upgrade weekend: Monday, 30% of Linux hosts show agent 'limited capability' — kernel module mismatch on the new kernel. The policy assumed full enforcement. The assessor asks for the postmortem.
evidence: The cause
Kernel-module mismatch: the agent's deep hooks didn't support the new LTS kernel. The upgrade changed the kernel; the agent's compatibility wasn't verified.
The planning failure
The kernel support matrix wasn't checked before the upgrade — the 'verify compatibility' step existed in the plan template and was skipped.
Now and next

Immediate: vendor's updated module (or pinned kernel) for the affected hosts, with the fleet's protection honestly reported as degraded meanwhile. Next: kernel-matrix verification becomes a hard gate on OS upgrades, tested in the pilot ring.
choices: The vendor's fault for slow kernel support

The upgrade skipped the kernel-compatibility gate: 30% of hosts run a mismatched agent module with degraded enforcement — remediate with the updated module (reporting honestly degraded meanwhile), and make kernel-matrix verification a hard upgrade gate tested in the pilot
Roll back the Ubuntu upgrade
Uninstall the agent from the affected hosts
scenarios.hint: Thirty percent 'limited capability' after a kernel change. What verification was skipped — and where should it have lived?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it names the skipped gate, remediates honestly (degraded status reported, not hidden), and hardens the process. A is wrong: the vendor's support pace doesn't excuse skipping your own compatibility check. C is wrong: rolling back an LTS upgrade fleet-wide over an agent module is disproportionate. D is wrong: uninstalling the agent 'fixes' the capability warning by removing protection.

scenarios.title: The dev who curl-pipes
scenarios.situation: A developer's standard workflow: curl vendor-install.sh | sudo bash — for tools, weekly. The allowlist blocks the downloaded payloads (unknown hashes); the dev demands an exception 'for productivity.' The assessor asks for your answer.
evidence: The practice
Curl-pipe-to-bash as root, weekly, from multiple vendors: unauthenticated code execution with full privileges — the supply-chain nightmare as a lifestyle.
The risk
One compromised vendor script (or one typosquatted URL) runs as root on a dev machine with source-code access. The allowlist is correctly blocking the unknown payloads.
The professional path

No exception for the practice: mirror the needed tools internally (vetted, hashed, allowlisted) or require signed packages via the package manager. 'Productivity' doesn't survive the first compromised script — and the dev gets a FASTER path (internal mirror) than the curl pipe.
choices: Grant the exception; developers need speed

Deny the exception: curl-pipe-to-bash as root is unauthenticated remote code execution — replace with an internal mirror of vetted tools (hashed, allowlisted) or signed packages via the package manager, which is also faster for the dev than the pipe
Allow it but log the scripts
Tell the dev to stop being difficult
scenarios.hint: Weekly unauthenticated root code execution from the internet. What would have to be true for an exception to be safe?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it refuses the practice (not the person), names the actual risk class, and provides the better path (internal mirror — faster AND safer). A is wrong: 'need speed' doesn't make remote root code execution acceptable. C is wrong: logging the compromise doesn't prevent it. D is wrong: dismissing the dev loses the chance to give them the better workflow.

scenarios.title: The log that stayed local
scenarios.situation: Incident on a Linux server: the team discovers the agent's logs were never forwarded — 6 months of deny history exists only on the box. The investigation needs fleet-wide correlation for the same indicators. The assessor asks for the finding.
evidence: The finding
6 months of unforwarded logs: the endpoint was monitored locally and blind centrally. Fleet-wide correlation — the exact capability the investigation needs — is impossible retroactively.
The cost
The current investigation is hamstrung (manual per-box collection), and 6 months of potential detections went uncorrelated. The blind spot is historical, not just current.
The fix

Immediate: forward now, backfill what can be collected. Systemic: log forwarding is a deployment checklist item (verified, not assumed), with a quarterly audit that forwarding is actually working — 'configured' is not 'flowing.'
choices: The incident is over; enable forwarding when convenient

Finding: 6 months of endpoint telemetry never left the box — the investigation can't correlate fleet-wide and months of detections went unanalyzed; fix by forwarding now, backfilling what exists, and making verified log flow a deployment checklist item with quarterly audits
Copy the logs manually for this incident
Increase local log retention
scenarios.hint: Six months of denies, one box, zero correlation. What was this endpoint — monitored, or just logging?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it distinguishes logging from monitoring, quantifies the cost (this investigation + 6 months of missed correlation), and makes forwarding a verified checklist item. A is wrong: 'when convenient' after the finding is how the next 6 months happen. C is wrong: manual copying serves this incident while the systemic blindness continues. D is wrong: longer local retention extends the unmonitored archive — the opposite of the fix.

domains.name: Uninstall Protection
domains.description: Keeping the agent on the endpoint: tamper protection, uninstall authorization workflows, and detecting removal attempts.

scenarios.title: The forum-post uninstall
scenarios.situation: Three users in one week: each disabled the agent following the same forum post ('fix slow PC: disable your security'). All three machines were unprotected for days; one now shows ransomware indicators. The assessor asks for the full response.
evidence: The immediate
One machine shows ransomware indicators: isolate it NOW, treat as an incident. The other two: verify clean, re-enable, investigate the unprotected window.
The control failure
Standard users could disable the agent: tamper protection is misconfigured or absent. The forum post worked because the control allowed it.
The systemic

Fix tamper protection (standard users cannot disable, period), alert on disable attempts, and address the 'slow PC' complaints that drove users to the forum — the bypass had a motive; fix the motive too.
choices: Punish the three users for disabling protection

Isolate the ransomware-indicator machine as an incident; verify and re-enable the other two with window investigation; fix tamper protection so standard users cannot disable; alert on attempts; and address the performance complaints that motivated the bypass — no punishment for the users, fix the control and the motive
Re-enable the agents and move on
Block the forum site
scenarios.hint: Three users, one forum post, one ransomware indicator. What failed — the users, or the control that let users disable it?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it prioritizes correctly (incident first), fixes the actual control failure (user-disable possible), adds detection, addresses the motive (slow PC), and refuses punishment (which teaches concealment). A is wrong: punishment blinds you to the next bypass. C is wrong: re-enabling without fixing tamper protection or investigating the windows changes nothing. D is wrong: blocking one forum doesn't un-teach the method or fix the control.

scenarios.title: The 3 AM SYSTEM uninstall attempt
scenarios.situation: Alert: 3:12 AM, server SRV-DB-02, uninstall attempt on the agent by NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, blocked by tamper protection. No ticket, no maintenance window. The assessor asks for your read.
evidence: The signals
3 AM + server + SYSTEM context + uninstall attempt + no ticket + no window: the tamper attempt used the highest-privilege context at the quietest hour with no authorization.
The read
SYSTEM-context uninstall attempts are not users troubleshooting: this is malware's standard first move (kill the protection) or a compromised maintenance script. Either way, incident-grade.
The response

Isolate the server, verify the agent is intact and enforcing, investigate what runs as SYSTEM (scheduled tasks, services), hunt for the delivery — the blocked attempt is a detection of an active attack step.
choices: The tamper protection worked; no action needed

Incident-grade: the 3 AM SYSTEM-context uninstall attempt with no ticket is malware's standard opening move — isolate the server, verify agent integrity, investigate SYSTEM-context actors (tasks, services), hunt the delivery; the blocked attempt is a detection, not a closed event
Whitelist the SYSTEM uninstall for maintenance
Reboot the server
scenarios.hint: Blocked by tamper protection at 3 AM from SYSTEM with no ticket. Is the story 'control worked' — or 'attack detected'?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it reads the signal cluster correctly (this is the attack pattern, not a maintenance pattern), responds as an incident, and treats the block as the detection it is. A is wrong: 'worked, closed' ignores that the attempt proves an active hostile actor on a database server. C is wrong: whitelisting SYSTEM uninstalls for 'maintenance' creates the exact hole the attacker wants. D is wrong: rebooting does nothing about the actor that attempted the uninstall.

scenarios.title: The migration's scripted removal
scenarios.situation: Migration project: 200 agents must be removed (vendor switch). The project plan says 'technicians will uninstall manually per machine.' The assessor asks for your review of the plan.
evidence: The plan's flaw
200 manual uninstalls: unscalable, unauditable, unverifiable — and each manual removal is a tamper-protection interaction performed by a human under time pressure.
The right method
Scripted authorized removal: console-driven or token-based mass uninstall, logged per machine, with verification (console confirms each removal). The workflow scales; humans don't.
The sequencing
Removal verified BEFORE new-agent install per machine (never unprotected-and-new-agent-less), in rings like any change, with the rollback being 'reinstall the old agent' — tested.
choices: Approve the manual plan; technicians are careful

Reject manual-per-machine: use scripted authorized removal (console/token-driven, logged per machine, verified per removal), sequenced in rings with removal-verified-before-install and a tested rollback — 200 manual uninstalls is 200 un-audited tamper events
Skip removal; install the new agent over the old
Let users uninstall it themselves to save time
scenarios.hint: Two hundred manual uninstalls. What is each one, from the tamper-protection log's perspective?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it identifies the scale/audit problem, prescribes the scripted authorized method, and sequences it safely. A is wrong: 'careful technicians' doesn't scale to 200 or produce an audit trail. C is wrong: installing over the old agent creates the conflict failure from the deployment domain. D is wrong: user self-service uninstall is the exact anti-pattern the domain prohibits.

scenarios.title: The admin who 'needed' to disable it
scenarios.situation: A domain admin disabled the agent on their workstation 'for troubleshooting' — no ticket, no token, and the tamper protection allowed it (admin bypass configured 'for IT convenience'). The machine was unprotected for 6 hours. The assessor asks for findings.
evidence: Finding 1
Admin bypass on tamper protection 'for convenience': the control was configured to not control the most capable actors. The bypass is the finding.
Finding 2
Unticketed 6-hour unprotected window on a domain admin's workstation: the highest-value target, unmonitored, by its owner's hand.
The fix

Remove the admin bypass (admins use the ticket+token workflow like everyone), alert on ALL tamper events including admin-initiated, and investigate the 6-hour window. Convenience is not a control rationale.
choices: The admin was troubleshooting; no issue

Two findings: the tamper protection's admin bypass ('for convenience') nullifies the control for the most capable actors, and a 6-hour unticketed unprotected window on a domain admin workstation — remove the bypass, require the workflow for admins too, alert on all tamper, investigate the window
Remove the admin's rights as punishment
The agent is too restrictive; loosen it
scenarios.hint: 'For IT convenience' — what does that phrase actually authorize, and for whom?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it names both findings, removes the bypass (the structural fix), and investigates the window. A is wrong: unticketed protection-disablement by a domain admin is never 'no issue.' C is wrong: punishment without fixing the bypass leaves the next admin the same hole. D is wrong: the agent wasn't restrictive — it was correctly protective until the bypass neutered it.

scenarios.title: The stale-green console
scenarios.situation: Incident review: a machine was compromised 3 weeks ago. The console showed it 'healthy' the entire time — because the agent was uninstalled on day 1, and the console displays last-known state indefinitely. The assessor asks for the systemic failure.
evidence: The failure
The console reports absence as health: an uninstalled agent renders as 'healthy (stale)' instead of alarming. The monitoring displays the opposite of reality.
The cost
3 weeks of assumed protection on a compromised machine: the incident's dwell time was manufactured by the console's silence.
The fix

Stale-agent alerting (no check-in for X hours = alert, not green), distinct console states (healthy / stale / uninstalled / never-seen), and the rule: absence of signal is a signal. Green must mean verified-current.
choices: The console is fine; the techs should have noticed

Systemic failure: the console displays uninstalled agents as healthy-stale, manufacturing 3 weeks of false assurance — fix with stale-agent alerting, distinct agent states, and the principle that absence of signal is itself a signal
Check consoles more often
The agent should be harder to uninstall
scenarios.hint: Three weeks 'healthy,' agent gone day one. What did the console actually report — and what should it have reported?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it identifies the display failure as systemic (not human), prescribes the alerting and state model, and states the principle. A is wrong: 'should have noticed' blames humans for a console that lied. C is wrong: more frequent checks of a lying console just observe the lie more often. D is wrong: harder uninstall doesn't fix the DISPLAY failure — a legitimately uninstalled agent would still show green.

scenarios.title: The break-glass request
scenarios.situation: 2 AM: ransomware is encrypting THROUGH the agent on a critical server (agent malfunction suspected). The on-call admin requests break-glass removal: 'I need the documented emergency uninstall NOW.' The assessor asks how break-glass should work.
evidence: When break-glass is legitimate
This is the case it exists for: the protection itself is implicated in an active incident, and standard removal is too slow or unavailable.
How it must work

Documented procedure + emergency authorization (two-person, even at 2 AM — wake someone) + time-limited effect + FULL audit (who, what, why, when) + mandatory post-incident review of the break-glass use itself.
The guardrail
Break-glass is rare, audited, and reviewed — every use triggers 'was this truly break-glass, or did the normal workflow fail?' If the normal workflow failed, fix THAT.
choices: Deny it; break-glass is too dangerous to ever use

Grant it under the documented emergency procedure: two-person authorization, time-limited, fully audited — then mandatory post-incident review of both the incident AND whether the break-glass use was truly necessary (or the normal workflow failed)
Give the admin the universal uninstall password
Approve it verbally and document later
scenarios.hint: The protection is implicated in an active incident at 2 AM. What makes break-glass SAFE to have — and safe to use?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it grants the legitimate emergency use under full guardrails (two-person, audited, time-limited) and — the maturity signal — reviews the break-glass use itself afterward. A is wrong: a break-glass that can never be used is a decoration; this is its exact use case. C is wrong: a universal password is the shared-secret failure. D is wrong: 'document later' for the highest-risk action is how accountability dies.

domains.name: Approval Center Ops
domains.description: Running the request queue: intake, evidence, decisions, SLAs, and turning the queue from a complaint box into a program instrument.

scenarios.title: The 120-ticket Monday
scenarios.situation: Monday 9 AM: 120 pending requests, oldest 11 days. Three departments now use 'VP email approval' instead. The helpdesk lead asks for the recovery plan.
evidence: The diagnosis
Unstaffed, unmeasured, no-SLA queue: the 11-day oldest is the metric. The organization routed around the failure with shadow approvals.
The triage
Sort by urgency-with-evidence first (real deadlines), then by age; kill duplicates; fast-lane the precedented. The backlog is triaged like an incident — because it is one.
The systemic
Publish the SLA, staff to it, absorb the shadow demand into the real process (the demand was legitimate), and add queue-depth alerting so 120 never accumulates silently again.
choices: Hire three more approvers today

Triage the backlog like an incident (urgent-with-evidence first, dedupe, fast-lane precedent), then publish and staff the SLA, absorb the legitimate shadow demand into the real workflow, and add queue-depth alerting
Auto-approve everything over 7 days old
Ban VP-email approvals immediately
scenarios.hint: One hundred twenty tickets, eleven days, shadow process running. Is this a staffing problem — or a process failure wearing a queue?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it triages the incident first, then fixes the process (SLA, staffing, absorption of real demand), and adds the alerting. A is wrong: hiring into a process without SLA or triage scales the failure. C is wrong: auto-approving aged requests converts backlog into unscoped decisions. D is wrong: banning the workaround without fixing the queue recreates it in weeks.

scenarios.title: The intake form from nowhere
scenarios.situation: Half the queue is 'it doesn't work' with no binary name, no error, no user context. Analysts spend hours per request on back-and-forth. The assessor asks for the fix.
evidence: The cost
Each bad-intake request costs hours of analyst back-and-forth: the queue's throughput is throttled by its intake, not its analysts.
The fix

Required intake fields: binary name/path, the exact block message or screenshot, business need, deadline, requester, ticket. Plus auto-triage: known-good precedents fast-lane, unknowns route to sandbox scheduling.
The principle
Intake quality is a design choice: every required field is analyst-hours saved. The form is the cheapest analyst you'll ever hire.
choices: Hire more analysts for the back-and-forth
Redesign intake: required fields (binary, block evidence, need, deadline, ticket) plus auto-triage rules (precedent fast-lane, unknown → sandbox) — intake quality is throughput
Reject all bad-intake requests
Call every requester for details
scenarios.hint: Half the queue is 'it doesn't work.' Is the bottleneck the analysts — or the intake?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it fixes the throughput constraint at its source (intake design) with both fields and auto-triage. A is wrong: more analysts doing back-and-forth scales the waste. C is wrong: mass rejection punishes users for the form's failure. D is wrong: calling every requester IS the back-and-forth, formalized.

scenarios.title: The precedent nobody wrote down
scenarios.situation: Same vendor tool, 15th request this quarter. Each was approved after a full 2-hour investigation — because no one documented the first one's findings. The assessor asks what the waste is and how to stop it.
evidence: The waste
14 redundant investigations: the signer was verified once (in effect, 15 times), the rule pattern re-derived each time. Hours of analyst time for zero new information.
The fix
Precedent records: vendor verified (signer, date, by whom), rule pattern set, fast-lane criteria defined ('same signer + same product line → verify hash, approve'). The 16th request takes 10 minutes.
The systemic
The approval record template includes a 'precedent' field: each decision notes whether it establishes or follows precedent. Knowledge compounds instead of evaporating.
choices: The investigations were thorough; no waste

Waste is 14 redundant re-investigations: create precedent records (verified signer, rule pattern, fast-lane criteria) so repeat requests ride the first one's work — and add 'precedent' to the decision record template
Stop approving the tool to end the requests
Assign all 15 to one analyst for consistency
scenarios.hint: Fifteen requests, fifteen full investigations, one vendor. What was re-derived fourteen times — and where should it have lived?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it quantifies the waste, creates the precedent mechanism, and templates it into the record. A is wrong: thoroughness repeated 15x without learning is toil, not rigor. C is wrong: denying a legitimate tool to save investigation time punishes the business for the knowledge gap. D is wrong: one analyst doing 15 redundant investigations is still 15 redundant investigations.

scenarios.title: The urgent that wasn't
scenarios.situation: 'URGENT' request: 'need this game installed for the team morale event Friday.' Binary: unsigned, from a personal file share. The requester marked it urgent and CC'd their manager. The assessor asks how urgency gets verified.
evidence: The urgency claim
'Morale event Friday' is a deadline, not a business urgency: no business function is blocked. Urgency definitions exist precisely for this.
The binary
Unsigned from a personal share: the evidence side is also red. Urgent-or-not, this binary needs the sandbox and the provenance check.
The response

Reclassify to standard (the urgency definition decides, not the caps lock), sandbox the binary per the unknown workflow, and communicate both plainly: 'I've queued this as standard — here's why, and here's the path.'
choices: Treat as urgent; the manager was CC'd

Verify against the urgency definition (no business function blocked → standard), run the unknown-binary workflow (sandbox + provenance) regardless of the flag, and communicate the reclassification plainly
Deny it for the caps lock
Approve it; morale matters
scenarios.hint: 'URGENT' in caps, manager CC'd, game binary from a file share. What verifies urgency — the formatting, or the definition?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it applies the urgency definition (not the formatting), runs the evidence workflow the binary requires, and communicates without condescension. A is wrong: CC'ing a manager doesn't convert a morale event into business urgency. C is wrong: denying for tone is unprofessional — decide on evidence and definitions. D is wrong: 'morale' doesn't verify an unsigned file-share binary.

scenarios.title: The deny that created shadow IT
scenarios.situation: Three months ago: a data-analysis tool was denied ('not on the approved list') with no explanation and no path. Today: the team runs it on personal laptops, emailing datasets to themselves. The assessor asks for the causal chain.
evidence: The chain
Unexplained deny → legitimate need unmet → work moves off-managed (personal laptops, email exfiltration of datasets) — the deny didn't stop the tool; it moved the DATA outside every control.
The irony
The control designed to protect data caused the data's exfiltration: the deny's missing path-to-yes is the incident's root cause.
The fix

Immediate: engage the team (what do they need? sanction a safe path — approved tool, VDI, whatever fits). Systemic: every deny carries the path to yes; measure deny-to-approval conversion; treat shadow IT as unmet-need signal.
choices: Punish the team for shadow IT

The unexplained deny moved legitimate work — and the datasets — outside all controls: engage the team to sanction a safe path now, and systemically require path-to-yes on every deny while treating shadow IT as unmet-need signal
Block personal laptops from the network
The deny was correct; the team was wrong
scenarios.hint: The deny 'worked' — and the datasets now live in personal email. What did the deny actually accomplish?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it traces the full causal chain (deny → unmet need → exfiltration), fixes forward (sanctioned safe path), and repairs the deny process. A is wrong: punishment for a need the process failed to serve teaches concealment. C is wrong: blocking personal laptops doesn't recall the emailed datasets. D is wrong: 'correct deny' with no path is what CAUSED the incident — correctness without usability is the failure.

scenarios.title: The metrics review
scenarios.situation: Quarterly: approval turnaround averaged 5.2h (SLA 4h), deny-to-approval conversion 70%, repeat-request rate 12%, queue depth never exceeded 30. The assessor asks: healthy or not, and what do you tune?
evidence: The read
Mostly healthy with one amber: turnaround 30% over SLA (mild breach), conversion 70% (paths work), repeats 12% (watch: some users loop), queue depth controlled (triage works).
The tune

Turnaround: find the slow segment (intake? evidence? approver availability?) — the breach is mild, so tune surgically. Repeats at 12%: sample them — are they the same apps (policy gap) or the same users (coaching)?
The report
'SLA amber at 5.2h vs 4h — investigating the slow segment; conversion healthy at 70%; repeats under review.' Honest, specific, owned — the metrics review the program, not the people.
scenarios.prompt: Healthy or not? What do you tune?
choices: Healthy; 5.2h is close enough to 4h

Mostly healthy, one amber: turnaround 30% over SLA needs surgical tuning (find the slow segment), repeats at 12% need sampling (policy gap or coaching?) — report honestly with the investigation plan; conversion and queue depth are green
Unhealthy; overhaul the whole process
The SLA is too strict; relax it to 6h
scenarios.hint: 5.2 vs 4.0, 70% conversion, 12% repeats. Which number is the amber — and what does 'tune' mean for it?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it reads each metric correctly, tunes surgically (not overhauls), and reports with the plan. A is wrong: 'close enough' normalizes the breach instead of investigating it. C is wrong: overhauling a mostly-healthy process for a 30% SLA miss is disproportionate. D is wrong: relaxing the SLA to meet the metric is grading your own homework.

domains.name: Testing Environment
domains.description: Detonate before you decide: the sandbox workflow, reading detonation reports, and knowing the sandbox's limits.

scenarios.title: The clean report with a dirty context
scenarios.situation: Sandbox report: CLEAN — updater installs, writes its own directory, reaches the vendor's documented CDN, no canary touches, no persistence. Context: the binary came from a personal file share, 'sent by a friend of the finance manager.' The assessor asks for your decision.
evidence: The report
Genuinely clean behavior: the binary does what an updater should, nothing it shouldn't. Strong evidence.
The context
Personal file share via 'a friend': the provenance is unverifiable and unofficial. A clean binary from a dirty channel is still a dirty channel — the NEXT binary from that friend may not be clean.
The decision

Deny this instance (unverifiable provenance — the channel, not the binary, fails), and give the path: 'get it from the vendor's official download; that's a 10-minute approval.' The sandbox cleared the binary; the provenance fails the request.
choices: Approve; the sandbox is clean

Deny this instance on provenance (personal file share via 'a friend' is unverifiable) while acknowledging the clean report — and provide the path: the official vendor download gets fast approval. The binary passed; the channel failed
Approve it but monitor the machine
Ban the finance manager's friend
scenarios.hint: Clean binary, dirty channel. Which one are you approving — the bytes, or the supply chain?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it separates binary evidence (clean) from provenance evidence (unverifiable), denies the instance on the right grounds, and provides the working path. A is wrong: approving blesses the file-share channel — the next binary from 'the friend' rides the precedent. C is wrong: 'approve but monitor' is approval with anxiety instead of a decision. D is wrong: the friend isn't the problem to solve; the channel is.

scenarios.title: The sleeper
scenarios.situation: Sandbox: CLEAN — 5-minute detonation, binary mostly idle. But: the binary contains an embedded scheduled task set for +6 hours, and imports networking functions it never used in the window. The assessor asks what the clean verdict is worth.
evidence: The signals
Scheduled task at +6h (past the 5-min window) + unused networking imports: the binary is built to act AFTER observation ends. Classic sleeper structure.
The clean verdict's worth
Worth exactly the 5 observed minutes: the verdict covers the window, not the binary. The +6h task is outside the verdict's jurisdiction.
The decision
Treat as suspicious: extend the detonation past the trigger, or deny pending the vendor's explanation of the scheduled task. 'Clean for 5 minutes' is not 'clean.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the clean verdict worth?
choices: Full approval; clean is clean

The 5-minute clean covers 5 minutes: the +6h scheduled task and unused network imports indicate sleeper structure — extend the detonation past the trigger or deny pending explanation; 'clean for 5 minutes' is not 'clean'
Approve with a 6-hour time-box
The imports are probably just unused code
scenarios.hint: Five clean minutes, a +6 hour trigger, unused network imports. What did the sandbox actually observe?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it bounds the verdict to the observed window, reads the sleeper structure correctly, and acts (extend or deny-pending-explanation). A is wrong: 'clean is clean' ignores that the verdict's jurisdiction ended at minute 5. C is wrong: a 6-hour time-box approves the binary to detonate on schedule. D is wrong: 'probably unused' is the assumption the sleeper relies on.

scenarios.title: The report nobody read
scenarios.situation: Approval granted for an unsigned tool: the ticket says 'sandboxed — clean.' The full report (never opened) shows: canary passwords.txt READ, registry Run key WRITTEN, outbound to a 4-day-old domain. The tool is now fleet-wide. The assessor asks for the failure.
evidence: The failure

Verdict-first approval: the approver read the summary word 'clean' (or the ticket's claim of it) without opening the behavior sections. The report CONTAINED the verdict — suspicious-to-malicious — in its sections.
The current state
A credential-reading, persistence-writing, new-domain-contacting binary is fleet-wide on a 'clean' ticket. This is now an incident, not a bad approval.
The response

Immediate: incident process (isolate sample, hunt the fleet, investigate the approver's other tickets). Systemic: approvals require the BEHAVIOR sections attested, not the verdict word — the ticket template changes.
choices: The sandbox is unreliable

The approver read the verdict word without the behavior sections — the report contained three hostile behaviors; the binary is now fleet-wide, so this is an incident (isolate, hunt, investigate the approver's other tickets), and the ticket template must require behavior-section attestation
Re-sandbox the binary
The tool is probably fine; canary reads happen
scenarios.hint: Canary passwords read, Run key written, 4-day-old domain — under a 'clean' ticket. What was actually read before approval?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it identifies the verdict-first failure precisely, escalates correctly (fleet-wide hostile binary = incident), and fixes the template. A is wrong: the sandbox worked perfectly — the human didn't read it. C is wrong: re-sandboxing answers nothing; the report already exists and already condemns. D is wrong: 'canary reads happen' normalizes the exact tripwire the canaries exist to trip.

scenarios.title: The queue for the sandbox
scenarios.situation: The sandbox queue: 40 submissions, 3-day wait. Analysts have started approving 'low-risk' unknowns without detonating ('it's just a PDF tool'). The assessor asks for the systemic fix.
evidence: The dynamic
Scarce sandbox capacity + queue pressure = analysts rationing evidence. 'Low-risk' is being decided by gut, which is exactly what the sandbox exists to replace.
The risk
The skipped detonations are unobserved unknowns entering the fleet on analyst intuition. The queue delay is being paid in unverified approvals.
The systemic fix

Triage the sandbox queue (urgent-with-evidence first, dedupe identical binaries), fast-lane the precedented (known-vendor patterns), and address capacity (more concurrent detonations or a second environment) — never normalize skipping. 'Just a PDF tool' detonates like everything else.
choices: Let analysts keep skipping low-risk ones; they have judgment

Triage the sandbox queue (urgent first, dedupe identicals), fast-lane precedented patterns, and fix capacity — 'low-risk' gut calls are what the sandbox replaces; normalizing skips converts the queue delay into unverified approvals
Ban PDF tools
Approve everything in the queue to clear it
scenarios.hint: Forty waiting, analysts skipping 'low-risk' ones. What is being rationed — and what is it being replaced with?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it treats the queue as a capacity problem (triage + fast-lane + capacity), not a judgment problem, and refuses to normalize skips. A is wrong: 'analyst judgment' for risk-classification is the gut-call the sandbox replaces. C is wrong: banning a category doesn't fix the queue. D is wrong: mass approval to clear a sandbox queue is the evidence-standard collapse.

scenarios.title: The vendor's 'don't sandbox us'
scenarios.situation: A vendor's support engineer: 'Don't detonate our installer in your sandbox — it phones home to our licensing and your sandbox will flag it. Just approve the hash.' The installer is signed by the vendor. The assessor asks for your response.
evidence: The request
'Don't verify us, trust us': the vendor asks you to skip your evidence process on their assurance. The licensing phone-home is EXPECTED behavior they could have documented.
The answer

You sandbox anyway — with the vendor's context noted ('expect licensing contact to X'). If the ONLY anomaly is the documented licensing call, the report supports approval. The sandbox doesn't distrust the vendor; it verifies the binary.
The principle
Your verification process is yours: vendors don't get vetoes over your evidence. A vendor threatened by your sandbox is telling you something — usually just impatience, but verify, don't obey.
choices: Obey the vendor; they know their installer

Detonate anyway with the vendor's context noted: if the only anomaly is the documented licensing call, approve on the evidence — your verification process doesn't take vendor vetoes; the sandbox verifies the binary, it doesn't insult the vendor
Approve the hash without detonating
Drop the vendor
scenarios.hint: 'Don't test our software, just trust us.' What is being asked — and what does your process answer?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it maintains verification independence while being fair (vendor context noted, documented licensing call expected), deciding on evidence. A is wrong: vendor assurance replaces your evidence process with their marketing. C is wrong: hash approval without detonation is exactly what was asked — and exactly what the process forbids for unknowns. D is wrong: dropping a needed vendor over a support engineer's impatience is disproportionate.

scenarios.title: The malicious report: now it's an incident
scenarios.situation: Sandbox report: MALICIOUS — mass file encryption behavior, canary documents encrypted, Run-key persistence, C2 to a known-bad domain. Submitted by: a finance user's request for 'the new payroll tool,' sourced from an email attachment. The assessor asks for the pivot.
evidence: The pivot
This stopped being an approval request the moment the report said MALICIOUS: it is now an active phishing-delivered ransomware incident. The approval workflow ends; the incident workflow begins.
The victim
The finance user is likely a victim (phished), not a perpetrator — but verify: how did the attachment arrive, did they execute anything, what else did they touch? Victim-first, verify-always.
The response

Isolate the user's machine (did anything execute outside the sandbox?), hunt the email delivery (who else got it?), block the C2 domain, notify and support the user — and thank them for submitting it instead of running it.
choices: Deny the request and close the ticket

Pivot to incident response: the MALICIOUS report ends the approval workflow — isolate the user's machine, verify nothing executed outside the sandbox, hunt the email delivery laterally, block the C2, and treat the user as a likely victim (support, verify, thank them for submitting instead of running it)
Approve it; the user needs the payroll tool
Delete the sandbox report
scenarios.hint: The report says MALICIOUS. What just ended — and what just began?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it pivots cleanly (approval → incident), covers the full response (isolate, verify, hunt, block), and handles the human correctly (victim-first, gratitude for submitting). A is wrong: 'deny and close' treats ransomware as a bad request — the delivery is still in the inbox. C is wrong: approving a MALICIOUS report is the catastrophic failure. D is wrong: deleting the report destroys the incident's foundational evidence.

domains.name: Unified Audit
domains.description: The source of truth for endpoint operations: reading audit entries, prevalence, retention, and turning logs into decisions.

scenarios.title: The 10-minute scan
scenarios.situation: Monday 8:00 AM audit scan: (a) updater.exe denied on 60 endpoints, signed Acme Inc; (b) 1 endpoint, 3 AM, rundll32 from temp, obfuscated; (c) new signer 'Acme Soft LLC' first-seen on 5 endpoints. The assessor asks for your triage of all three.
evidence: (a) 60 + signed
Systemic: version churn or rule error — central fix (certificate rule), not 60 investigations.
(b) 1 + 3AM + obfuscated
Targeted: incident-grade — isolate and investigate the box NOW. Highest priority.
(c) new signer, 5 endpoints
Unknown signer: verify the signer before anything executes further — hold, investigate the publisher, sandbox the binaries.
scenarios.prompt: Triage all three, in priority order.
choices: (a) first — 60 users are blocked

Priority: (b) isolate immediately (incident-grade: 3 AM obfuscated rundll32), then (c) hold and verify the unknown signer, then (a) central rule fix for the 60 — severity orders the work, not user count
(c) first — new signers are exciting
Handle them in alphabetical order
scenarios.hint: Sixty blocked users vs one 3 AM obfuscated rundll32. What orders the work — count, or severity?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it prioritizes by severity (incident first), sequences correctly (isolate → verify signer → central fix), and states the principle. A is wrong: user count doesn't outrank an active intrusion indicator. C is wrong: 'exciting' isn't a triage criterion. D is wrong: alphabetical triage is the abdication of judgment.

scenarios.title: The edited history
scenarios.situation: Investigation finds: an admin's account edited audit entries to hide their own policy change (which caused an outage). The audit system allowed edits by admins. The assessor asks for the findings.
evidence: Finding 1
The audit is editable by admins: history can be revised. Every past investigation's evidence is now questionable — the integrity failure is retroactive.
Finding 2
The admin's outage-causing change was hidden: the cover-up compounds the original failure, and the motive (hiding a mistake) suggests a blame culture worth addressing.
The fix

Tamper-evident audit (append-only, admin actions separately logged and uneditable), investigate the admin's full history, and address the culture: mistakes reported are fixable; mistakes hidden are incidents.
choices: The admin made a mistake; move on

Two findings: the audit's editability destroys historical evidence integrity (retroactive), and the hidden change compounds the outage — fix with tamper-evident audit design, investigate the admin's history, and address the blame culture that made hiding preferable to reporting
Fire the admin immediately
Restore the edited entries from backup
scenarios.hint: An editable audit. What does that do to EVERY investigation that ever used it?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it grasps the retroactive integrity failure, compounds correctly (cover-up > mistake), and fixes both the technical and cultural causes. A is wrong: 'a mistake' ignores the deliberate history-editing. C is wrong: immediate firing skips the history investigation the integrity failure demands. D is wrong: restoring entries doesn't fix the editability — the next edit is still possible.

scenarios.title: The retention gap
scenarios.situation: Auditor asks for Q1 audit data. Retention is 90 days; it's now Q3. The Q1 data is gone. The assessor asks: what failed, and when should it have been caught?
evidence: What failed
Retention shorter than the question cycle: auditors ask about quarters past, and 90 days doesn't cover Q1-from-Q3. The retention policy was designed without the compliance calendar.
When it should have been caught
At policy design (retention vs audit cycle), at the quarterly self-audit (the gap was visible every quarter), and at every storage-budget review. Three chances, all missed.
Now
Honest answer to the auditor ('retention was 90 days; Q1 is unavailable — here is what we have and the remediation'), then fix retention to cover the audit cycle plus margin, with restore testing.
scenarios.prompt: What failed, and when should it have been caught?
choices: The auditor is being unreasonable

Retention (90d) was designed without the audit cycle (quarters): the gap was catchable at policy design, at every quarterly self-audit, and at budget reviews — answer the auditor honestly with available data plus remediation, then fix retention to cover the cycle with margin
Recreate the Q1 data from memory
Blame the storage budget
scenarios.hint: Ninety-day retention, quarterly auditors. At what point was the arithmetic knowable?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it does the arithmetic, names the three missed catches, handles the auditor honestly, and fixes forward. A is wrong: the auditor's cycle is the requirement; the retention is what failed it. C is wrong: recreating audit data from memory is fabrication. D is wrong: the budget didn't set the retention policy — the design did.

scenarios.title: The correlated pair
scenarios.situation: Same host, same hour: ringfence deny (winword.exe → powershell.exe) AND firewall deny (winword.exe → no-history IP). Two separate analysts each closed their own ticket ('policy working as designed'). The assessor asks for the failure.
evidence: The failure
Siloed triage: two analysts each saw half an intrusion pattern and closed it. The correlation — same host, same hour, two dimensions — was nobody's job.
What the pair means
Coordinated malicious behavior: document-delivered, escape-attempted, egress-attempted. Each deny alone is a policy event; together they're an incident.
The fix

Immediate: reopen as an incident (isolate, investigate the document, hunt the delivery). Systemic: correlated-signal escalation rules (same host + same hour + 2+ dimensions → incident), and cross-domain audit review in the daily scan.
choices: No failure; both analysts were correct

Failure is siloed triage: the correlated pair (same host/hour, two dimensions) is an intrusion pattern neither analyst saw whole — reopen as an incident immediately, and build correlated-signal escalation into the daily scan
The analysts should be retrained
The policies are too noisy
scenarios.hint: Two tickets, two 'working as designed,' one intrusion. What was nobody's job?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it names the silo failure precisely, reopens correctly, and builds the systemic fix (correlation rules in the scan). A is wrong: each half-answer was correct and the whole was missed — that IS the failure. C is wrong: retraining individuals doesn't fix a process with no correlation step. D is wrong: the policies weren't noisy; the triage was blind.

scenarios.title: The first-seen Friday
scenarios.situation: Friday 4 PM: audit shows 'first seen in fleet' for 12 binaries, all signed by a new vendor the company just contracted. The vendor's deployment starts Monday. The assessor asks for the weekend plan.
evidence: The situation
12 first-seen binaries from a contracted vendor, deployment Monday: the Monday ticket avalanche is visible from Friday — if nothing is done.
The weekend plan

Verify the vendor's signer NOW (publisher identity, certificate validity), pre-build the scoped certificate rules, stage them for Monday, brief the helpdesk on the expected (non-)event. The weekend turns Monday's avalanche into a non-event.
The principle
First-seen is a signal, not a verdict — and a PLANNED first-seen (contracted vendor, known deployment) is a preparation opportunity, not a surprise.
choices: Wait for Monday and handle the tickets
Verify the vendor's signer now, pre-build and stage the scoped certificate rules for Monday, brief the helpdesk — turn the predictable first-seen wave into a non-event instead of a ticket avalanche
Block the vendor's binaries until reviewed
Enjoy the weekend; Monday's tickets are normal
scenarios.hint: Twelve first-seens, deployment Monday, and it's Friday. Is Monday's avalanche inevitable — or is it a choice?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it uses the weekend as preparation time (verify, pre-build, brief), converting the predictable wave into a non-event. A is wrong: 'handle the tickets' accepts a preventable avalanche. C is wrong: blocking a contracted vendor's deployment over plannable first-seens is the failure to prepare, formalized. D is wrong: normalizing preventable ticket avalanches is operational surrender.

scenarios.title: The audit question you can't answer
scenarios.situation: Self-audit: 'Were there unapproved executions on the lab machines in Q2?' The lab machines' agents were in monitor-only all quarter (no enforcement), and 3 lab machines never had agents installed. The assessor asks for the honest answer.
evidence: The honest answer

'We cannot fully answer: monitor-only doesn't block (so 'unapproved execution' is unmeasurable there), and 3 machines had no agent at all. Here's what we CAN show...' — the gap stated plainly, with the partial evidence offered.
Why honesty wins
The auditor (or assessor) will find the gap; stating it first with a remediation plan ('lab enforcement scheduled Q4, agents on all lab machines by [date]') converts a finding into a plan.
The lesson
Self-audits exist to find exactly this: the question you can't answer is the program gap. The lab's monitor-only-forever was the finding, waiting for the question.
choices: Yes, there were no unapproved executions — the audit shows none

'We cannot fully answer: monitor-only doesn't enforce and 3 machines lack agents — here's the partial evidence we have, the gap stated plainly, and the remediation (lab enforcement + full agent coverage by [date])'
Refuse to answer; the question is unfair
Estimate based on the other machines
scenarios.hint: Monitor-only all quarter, three machines agentless. What is the honest answer to 'were there unapproved executions?'
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it states the unanswerability plainly, offers the partial evidence, and converts the gap into a dated plan — the complete professional handling. A is wrong: 'the audit shows none' when the audit couldn't show it is the fabrication the scenario tests. C is wrong: refusing the question doesn't remove the gap. D is wrong: estimating unmeasured machines is invention.

domains.name: Incident Workflows
domains.description: When operations becomes response: the operator's role in incidents, containment with endpoint controls, and the handoff to the IR team.

scenarios.title: The 3 AM page: ransomware signals
scenarios.situation: 3:07 AM page: 4 hosts show mass file-encryption behavior + canary trips in the audit. You're the operator on call. The IR lead is 20 minutes out. The assessor asks for your first 20 minutes.
evidence: Minutes 0-5
Verify the signal (audit: 4 hosts, encryption behavior, canary trips — real), declare the incident per the escalation path, start the clock.
Minutes 5-15
Contain with the toolkit: network-quarantine the 4 hosts via policy (mgmt plane excepted), emergency hash-block the binary fleet-wide, kill the observed egress destinations. Ticketed, time-boxed.
Minutes 15-20
Freeze evidence (export the 4 hosts' audit histories), note the timeline so far, brief the IR lead on arrival: '4 hosts quarantined, hash blocked fleet-wide, evidence frozen, timeline started 03:07.'
choices: Wait for the IR lead; don't touch anything

Verify, declare, contain (quarantine the 4 via policy, fleet-wide hash block, egress kill — ticketed and time-boxed), freeze evidence, and brief the IR lead on arrival with the timeline — the operator's seat is containment + evidence, executed before the cavalry arrives
Start hunting for patient zero yourself
Shut down the 4 hosts remotely
scenarios.hint: Four hosts encrypting, IR 20 minutes out. What is YOUR seat — and what does it do first?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it executes the operator's seat completely (verify, declare, contain with the toolkit, freeze evidence, brief) — speed on controls, completeness on evidence, no freelancing. A is wrong: 20 minutes of uncontained ransomware is the abdication the scenario tests. C is wrong: hunting is the IR team's job; the operator's job is containment + evidence. D is wrong: shutdown destroys volatile evidence and kills the reporting the quarantine preserves.

scenarios.title: The quarantine that broke the business
scenarios.situation: You quarantined 10 hosts during an incident (correct call). One runs the warehouse management system; the warehouse is now idle, $50k/hour. The IR lead says 'keep them isolated.' Operations VP says 'restore it now.' The assessor asks how you handle the conflict.
evidence: The stakes
Real money vs real containment: both claims are legitimate. This is the incident's hardest judgment call, and it's yours to frame (not necessarily to make alone).
The options

Keep isolated (safest, costs $50k/h), restore with enhanced monitoring (scoped risk: the host rejoins with full audit + network watch), or partial restore (warehouse function via a clean spare while the host stays quarantined).
The process

Frame the options with costs for the incident commander — the COMMANDER decides, not the VP and not you alone. Your job: the options, the costs, the recommendation (partial restore), and the documented decision. Never let the VP override the commander directly.
choices: Restore it; $50k/hour is too much
Keep it isolated; the IR lead outranks the VP

Frame the three options (isolated / monitored-restore / partial-restore-via-spare) with costs for the incident commander to decide — recommend the spare-based partial restore, document the decision; the commander decides, pressure doesn't
Let the VP and IR lead argue it out
scenarios.hint: $50k/hour vs containment. Who decides — and what is your job in the decision?
scenarios.why: Correct is C: it structures the decision for the incident commander (options + costs + recommendation), protects the chain of command, and documents — neither the VP's money nor the IR lead's rank decides unilaterally. A is wrong: the $50k/hour cost doesn't unilaterally override containment — that's the commander's call with full options on the table. B is wrong: the IR lead's rank doesn't unilaterally override business continuity either; the commander weighs both legitimate claims. D is wrong: 'let them argue' is abdication — framing the decision with options, costs, and a recommendation is your job.

scenarios.title: The evidence you almost filtered
scenarios.situation: Exporting the incident evidence packet, you notice 200 'noise' denies from the compromised host — a misconfigured internal tool spamming blocks for weeks. You're tempted to exclude them ('they're irrelevant'). The assessor asks: include or exclude?
evidence: The temptation
The 200 denies are noise for YOUR triage — but the IR team reads noise differently: the misconfigured tool's behavior is baseline context, and 'irrelevant' is your judgment, not theirs.
The rule

Export the FULL relevant history: your triage notes accompany the packet with your read ('200 denies are the known misconfigured tool, see ticket X'), but the data goes unfiltered. The IR team finds things in what you filtered.
The custody
Note the export's scope and your annotation in the custody record: 'full host history exported; analyst note flags the 200 tool-spam denies.' Transparency, not editing.
choices: Exclude them; they're noise

Include the full history unfiltered, with your triage note annotating the 200 as the known tool-spam (ticket X) — the IR team gets complete data plus your read; filtering is editing, and editing destroys trust in the packet
Include them but don't mention it
Summarize the 200 as one line
scenarios.hint: Your noise, their baseline context. Whose judgment decides what's 'irrelevant'?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it keeps the data complete, adds the analyst's read as annotation (not deletion), and records it in custody. A is wrong: excluding is editing evidence — the IR team can't find what isn't there. C is wrong: silent inclusion without the annotation wastes their time re-deriving your known. D is wrong: summarizing 200 events as one line is filtering with extra steps.

scenarios.title: The freelance forensic adventure
scenarios.situation: Mid-incident, a talented operator starts their own forensic deep-dive on the compromised host — memory dumps, custom scripts — instead of their assigned containment tasks. Their findings are interesting. The quarantine rules aren't written yet. The assessor asks for your call as the shift lead.
evidence: The problem
Interesting findings, wrong seat: the containment tasks (quarantine rules, hash blocks) are undone while forensics — the IR team's job — gets duplicated. The incident's critical path is starving.
The call
Redirect immediately and kindly: 'Great instincts — log what you found, hand it to the IR lead, and I need those quarantine rules NOW.' Talent serves the incident's needs, not its curiosity.
The systemic
Role cards and the 'stay in your seat' brief at incident start: the shift lead assigns seats explicitly, and freelancing gets redirected at the first sign — kindly the first time, firmly after.
choices: Let them continue; the findings are valuable

Redirect kindly but immediately: log the findings, hand them to the IR lead, and return to the assigned containment tasks — the incident's critical path (quarantine, blocks) is starving while forensics gets duplicated; talent serves the incident's needs
Praise them publicly as an example
Reassign them to the IR team
scenarios.hint: Interesting findings, unbuilt quarantine rules. What is starving — and what is being fed?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it redirects without crushing (log it, hand it over), names the starvation (containment undone), and keeps the talent in its seat. A is wrong: 'valuable findings' don't excuse abandoning the critical path — the quarantine rules are the incident's priority. C is wrong: praising the freelancing teaches the whole shift to freelance. D is wrong: mid-incident reassignment is chaos; redirect within the structure.

scenarios.title: The postmortem with no changes
scenarios.situation: Postmortem for last month's incident concludes: 'Response was good, no changes needed.' But the timeline shows 3 hours from signal to containment, the runbook's quarantine step was improvised, and the same detection gap existed in the previous incident. The assessor asks for your response.
evidence: The failures
Three: 3h signal-to-containment (slow), improvised quarantine (runbook failed), repeat detection gap (previous incident taught nothing). 'No changes needed' contradicts the timeline.
The response

Reopen the postmortem with the timeline as the agenda: containment-time target, runbook fix (the improvised step gets written properly), detection-gap rule (the missed signal becomes a rule). 'No changes needed' is never the conclusion — always.
The culture
Postmortems that can't find improvements are postmortems protecting feelings. The shift lead models it: 'here's what I was slow on' — candor from the top licenses candor from everyone.
choices: Accept it; the team feels good about the response

Reopen with the timeline as agenda: 3h containment needs a target and a plan, the improvised runbook step gets written properly, the repeat detection gap becomes a rule — 'no changes needed' is never the conclusion; model the candor yourself
Criticize the team for the 3 hours
Skip postmortems; they demoralize
scenarios.hint: Three hours, improvised runbook, repeat gap — and 'no changes needed.' What does that sentence protect?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it uses the timeline to reopen honestly, converts each failure into a concrete improvement, and models the candor. A is wrong: accepting it protects feelings at the cost of the next incident's 3 hours. C is wrong: criticism without the improvement plan is just blame. D is wrong: skipping postmortems guarantees the repeat gap repeats again.

scenarios.title: The drill that found the gap
scenarios.situation: Quarterly incident drill: simulated ransomware, 4 'compromised' hosts. The operator freezes — can't find the quarantine button, the hash-block workflow needs a ticket they can't file mid-drill, evidence export takes 40 minutes. The assessor asks: drill failure or drill success?
evidence: The answer
Drill SUCCESS: the drill found three real gaps (console unfamiliarity, ticket-gated emergency workflow, 40-min evidence export) in a safe environment. A drill that finds nothing tested nothing.
The gaps
Quarantine must be muscle memory (console drills monthly), emergency workflows can't require normal tickets (break-glass procedure), evidence export must be scripted (40 min is 39 too many).
The follow-through
Each gap gets an owner and a date: console drills on the calendar, break-glass documented, export scripted and tested. The NEXT drill verifies the fixes — drills are a loop, not an event.
choices: Failure; the operator wasn't ready

Success: the drill exposed three real gaps (quarantine unfamiliarity, ticket-gated emergency workflow, 40-minute evidence export) safely — now each gets an owner, a fix, and a verification in the next drill; drills are a loop
Failure; drills should be realistic enough to pass
Blame the operator for freezing
scenarios.hint: Three gaps found, zero production impact. What is a drill FOR?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it understands the drill's purpose (finding gaps safely), converts each gap into owned fixes, and closes the loop with the next drill. A is wrong: 'wasn't ready' is the drill's FINDING, not its failure — the drill worked. C is wrong: drills realistic enough to always pass are theater. D is wrong: the freeze exposed the training gap; blaming the person wastes the lesson.

lessons.title: Default-deny operations: from Learning Mode to least privilege
concepts: Default-deny vs default-allow: approve the finite known-good list instead of chasing the infinite known-bad list
Rule strength: certificate > hash > path — never path rules in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both
Ringfencing’s four leashes: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Elevation is just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, and logged — never standing admin
Storage by serial, network by destination; assume breach throughout

example.code:
sha256sum AcmeUpdater.msi
# <hash>  AcmeUpdater.msi   — the hash names the bytes, not the trust
grep ERROR logs/app.log
# read the exact denial/failure lines BEFORE writing any rule
example.walkthrough: Hash the file to establish identity, then read the exact log lines before writing any rule. Rules come from evidence — the signature, the hash, the blocked child process — never from the ticket title or the requester’s urgency. This is the habit every scenario in this domain is testing.

pitfalls: Approving by path in user-writable directories — the weakest rule where it matters most
Leaving Installation or Learning Mode on indefinitely — an open gate with no timer
Writing global rules for one user’s request — scope is the whole discipline
lessons.try_it: Pick one scenario in this domain and write the rule you would create: rule type (certificate/hash/path), exact scope, and one sentence on why that type.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Tl Endpoint Ops move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Zero Trust Endpoint Operations
concepts: Zero Trust Endpoint Operations is a multi-step process within Zero Trust Endpoint Operations: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect Zero Trust Endpoint Operations to the broader Zero Trust Endpoint Operations ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  Zero Trust Endpoint Operations begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion
  Final state reached — how do you verify?
example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to Zero Trust Endpoint Operations. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating Zero Trust Endpoint Operations as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard the full Zero Trust Endpoint Operations flow from memory. Label every handoff and dependency.

lessons.title: How this bootcamp is built (and how to move through it)
concepts: This bootcamp has four moving parts: Lessons teach operations concepts, Scenarios put you in the operator's chair for realistic decisions, Labs build hands-on reps in a simulated shell, and the Mock Assessment measures readiness under time pressure.

Domains group the material by operational topic — deployment, baselining, tuning, overrides, platform coverage, and incident workflows. Work them in order first, then loop back to your weakest domains.
Scenarios are the core: each hands you evidence, a prompt, and four options. Read the EVIDENCE before the choices, decide like the operator on shift, and study the 'why' after — especially on misses.
The Mock Assessment domain assembles scenarios from every domain at runtime. Use it for timed full runs after the domains, not for first learning.

example.code:
SESSION (60 min)
  1. Read 2 lessons in one domain        (20 min)
  2. Work 3 scenarios, untimed             (20 min)
  3. Re-work every miss using the 'why'    (15 min)
  4. Log one line: what fooled you         ( 5 min)
example.walkthrough: Run every session in this shape. The reading builds the operations vocabulary, the scenarios build the on-shift judgment, and the re-work converts each miss into a permanent lesson. The one-line log compounds across sessions into your personal trap catalog.

pitfalls: Skipping the 'why' review — the mistake then repeats on assessment day.
Doing scenarios before the lessons — you burn test items without the framework to learn from them.
Using the Mock Assessment to learn instead of to measure — it measures readiness; it does not teach.
lessons.try_it: Run one 60-minute session today in exactly this shape and write your one-line log entry.

lessons.title: The operator's study loop: learn, drill, mock, review
concepts: Operations judgment is built in a loop: LEARN the concept, DRILL it in scenarios, MOCK it under time, REVIEW the misses — then repeat on the weak spots the review exposed.
Untimed drilling builds accuracy; timed mocking builds on-shift accuracy under pressure. They are different skills. Do not skip the timed phase.
Three 45-minute sessions across three days beat one 3-hour cram session. Judgment skills consolidate between sessions, not during them.
Bucket every miss: knowledge gap (didn't know it), reading gap (missed evidence), or pressure gap (knew it, picked fast). Fix the bucket, not just the question.
Any domain under 80% accuracy after two passes gets re-studied from the lessons — not re-drilled. Re-drilling a misunderstood concept just rehearses the misunderstanding.

example.code:
LOOP
  learn  -> read domain lessons, notes in your own words
  drill  -> 5-8 scenarios untimed, target 80%+
  mock   -> timed mixed run, on-shift pacing
  review -> bucket every miss, re-study weak domains
  repeat -> loop only on domains still under 80%
example.walkthrough: Each loop should shrink the weak-domain set. If a domain stays weak after two loops, slow down: re-read the lessons, write your own examples, explain the concept aloud — then drill again.

pitfalls: Memorizing scenario answers across repeats — mix domains to force real judgment.
Treating 80% untimed as ready — timed accuracy runs lower; confirm under the clock.
Reviewing only misses — also review the ones you got right for shaky reasons.
lessons.try_it: Pick your weakest domain after today's session and run one full loop on it tomorrow.

lessons.title: What endpoint-operations assessments test
concepts: They test the operator's judgment: given a deployment problem, a tuning decision, an override request, or a 2 AM page — what do you do, in what order, and why?

Recurring themes: staged rollout discipline (never big-bang), evidence-before-verdict triage, narrowest-sufficient change, least-privilege overrides, and the communication that keeps security and usability from becoming enemies.
Assessors score the ORDER of your thinking: observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate twice, document. Leading with the action before the evidence is the most common failure.

They also test what you do NOT do: no disabling controls to clear symptoms, no global approvals for local problems, no permanent exceptions for temporary needs. The wrong answers are always tempting shortcuts.

example.code:
OPERATOR'S RUBRIC
  + evidence cited before conclusion
  + staged, never big-bang
  + narrowest change that solves it
  + validated twice (good path + bad path)
  + documented for the next shift
  - control disabled to clear a symptom
  - global/permanent for local/temporary
example.walkthrough: Read this rubric before every scenario. The option that satisfies all five positives — and none of the negatives — is the answer. Narrating the rubric aloud is what earns partial credit when you are unsure.

pitfalls: Memorizing feature lists — assessments test what you DO with the features.
Treating every scenario as trivia — most test tradeoffs between defensible options.
Ignoring the business impact — the night shift idle is part of the judgment.
lessons.try_it: Re-answer one completed scenario aloud as if narrating to an assessor, using the rubric.

lessons.title: On-shift readiness checklist
concepts: Before the assessment: stop drilling two hours before sleep, review your miss log once, and settle logistics. Judgment degrades under cramming and fatigue.
Pacing: 5-8 minutes per scenario is the design target. At 10 minutes on one item, pick your best-supported answer and move on — one stuck question must not eat two others.
Read all evidence blocks fully before the choices. Choices reward skimmers; evidence rewards readers.
When evidence is thin, state your assumption and pick the least-privilege option. 'Assuming X, the narrowest safe action is Y' is a complete professional answer.
Afterward, write down every question you remember while fresh. That debrief is your study plan whether you pass or retake.

example.code:
DAY-OF SEQUENCE
  1. Arrive early, settle, breathe
  2. Skim all items: mark easy / medium / hard
  3. Easy first (bank points + confidence)
  4. Medium next, evidence-first reading
  5. Hard last, assumption stated, least privilege
  6. Reserve 10 min: review flagged items only
example.walkthrough: This sequence prevents the classic failure: burning 25 minutes on question 3 and rushing the ten you knew. Banked easy points steady your nerves, which measurably improves judgment on the hard items.

pitfalls: Changing answers on review without new evidence — first evidence-based instincts are usually right.
Leaving items blank — a reasoned guess beats a blank every time.
Bringing prohibited aids — know the rules before the day.
lessons.try_it: Do one full timed mock run this week using the day-of sequence, then write your debrief.

lessons.title: Capstone part 1: the fleet rollout plan
concepts: Your capstone: act as the endpoint-operations lead for 'Harbor Dental' (25 users, one site, mixed Windows/macOS). Deliverable one is the rollout plan: from agent deployment to full enforcement.

Structure it in waves: WAVE 0 (pilot — IT, 5 machines, 2 weeks), WAVE 1 (departments with complete inventories), WAVE 2 (everyone else). Each wave needs entry criteria (inventory complete, exceptions process staffed) and exit criteria (block rate stable, SLA met).
Include the deployment mechanics: agent install method per OS, deployment rings, health verification (check-in rate target: 99%+), and the rollback plan per wave.
Name the communications: what users are told before each wave, what the block message says, where the approval requests go, and the published SLA. A rollout plan without comms is a revolt plan.

example.code:
DELIVERABLE 1 — rollout-plan.md
  ## Wave structure + entry/exit criteria per wave
  ## Deployment mechanics per OS (method, rings, health checks)
  ## Learning/baseline windows per wave
  ## Communications (pre-wave, block message, SLA)
  ## Rollback plan per wave
example.walkthrough: Write it as if the assessor will execute it: every wave needs its gates, every gate needs its evidence. Vague waves ('then we roll out to everyone') score zero.

pitfalls: Big-bang waves — one wave's lessons must improve the next.
Entry criteria without evidence — 'inventory complete' needs the inventory attached.
No rollback plan — the plan you need most is the one you test least.
lessons.try_it: Draft Harbor Dental's wave structure tonight: waves, gates, and the comms per wave.

lessons.title: Capstone part 2: a week on the queue
concepts: Deliverable two: operate the endpoint-ops queue for a simulated week. You will handle (or invent realistically) 15 items: deployment failures, override requests, tuning decisions, a macOS gap, an uninstall attempt, and one genuine incident.
For each item: triage (scope, observe, hypothesize), act (narrowest safe change), validate twice (good path works, bad path denied), document (the note the next shift needs).
Score yourself with the operator's rubric. Any item where you disabled a control, approved globally, or skipped validation is a failed item — redo it.
End the week with the ops report: queue volume, mean time to resolve, repeat rate, and one process improvement you would implement. Operators who measure their own work get promoted.

example.code:
QUEUE ITEM TEMPLATE
  item:    override request, unsigned tool, dev team
  triage:  scope/observe/hypothesize (3 lines)
  action:  narrowest safe change + ticket
  validate: good path OK / bad path denied
  doc:     note for next shift
example.walkthrough: Fill one template per item. The template IS the discipline: it forces the order (triage before action, validation before close) that assessments test under time pressure.

pitfalls: Acting before triaging — the template's order is the skill.
Closing without the validation pair — 'user says it works' is half a validation.
Skipping the doc — the next shift inherits your undocumented work.
lessons.try_it: Write three queue items using the template: one override, one tuning decision, one deployment failure.

lessons.title: Capstone part 3: the operations review
concepts: Deliverable three: the quarterly operations review for Harbor Dental's endpoint program. Audience: the practice owner (non-technical) and your assessor (technical). One document, two readers.

Structure: posture summary (plain language), metrics with trends (block rate, approval turnaround, agent health, repeat rate), top 3 findings with evidence, top 3 recommendations sequenced by risk-per-effort, and residual risks stated honestly.
