  0 + signed-known -> probable legit new version
example.walkthrough: Let prevalence direct the response: high-plus-signed gets the central rule fix, low-plus-unsigned gets the box investigation, first-seen gets the sandbox queue. The fleet is talking — the operator listens first.

pitfalls: Troubleshooting 200 machines for a rule error — fix centrally.
Treating first-seen as guilty — new-to-fleet is a signal, not a verdict.
Ignoring prevalence entirely — the fleet is talking; listen.
lessons.try_it: Classify five invented audit entries by prevalence read alone.

lessons.title: Retention, integrity, and the auditor
concepts: Retention: the audit must cover the periods you'll be asked about (quarters, incident windows). Define it, fund the storage, TEST restores — an audit you can't query is an archive, not a control.
Integrity: audit logs must be tamper-evident (ideally tamper-proof): append-only, access-controlled, with admin actions themselves audited. An attacker who can edit the audit can edit history.

The auditor's questions: 'show me no unapproved execution in Q3' (the negative: deny coverage + policy completeness) and 'show me every exception's approval' (the positive: the register). Both come from this audit plus the exception records.
Self-audit quarterly: ask the auditor's questions of yourself before they do. The gaps you find are remediation; the gaps they find are findings.

example.code:
AUDIT HYGIENE
  retention: defined, funded, restore-tested
  integrity:  append-only, admin actions audited
  auditor:    negative (no unapproved exec) + positive (exceptions)
  self-audit: quarterly, before they do
example.walkthrough: Design retention around the questions you'll be asked, make the audit tamper-evident, and self-audit quarterly. The auditor's two proofs — the negative and the positive — come from this audit plus the exception register.

pitfalls: Untested restores — the archive you can't query.
Editable audits — history the attacker can revise.
Annual scramble — hygiene is continuous, not seasonal.
lessons.try_it: Check your posture: retention period? restore tested? admin actions audited?

lessons.title: From audit to action: the ops loop
concepts: The daily audit loop: SCAN (10-min pattern read: clusters? anomalies? new first-seens?), TRIAGE (systemic → rule fix; targeted → investigate; unknown → sandbox), ACT (ticketed, narrow), VERIFY (did the pattern change tomorrow?).
The scan is pattern-first: same binary many endpoints, same endpoint many binaries, new signer first-seen, odd-hour activity. Ten minutes of pattern reading beats an hour of ticket order.
Close the loop visibly: yesterday's systemic fix should move today's numbers. If the pattern persists after the fix, the fix was wrong — the audit tells you, if you look. The loop is the learning.

Escalation from the audit: correlated signals (ringfence deny + egress deny, same host, same hour) escalate to incident WITHOUT waiting for a ticket. The audit is a detection source, not just a record.

example.code:
DAILY AUDIT LOOP
  scan:    10-min pattern read (clusters, anomalies, first-seens)
  triage:  systemic->rule | targeted->investigate | unknown->sandbox
  act:     ticketed, narrow
  verify:  did the pattern move tomorrow?
  escalate: correlated signals -> incident, no ticket needed
example.walkthrough: Run the daily loop: ten-minute pattern scan, triage by pattern type, ticketed narrow action, and verify tomorrow that the pattern moved. Correlated signals escalate to incident directly — the audit is a detection source.

pitfalls: Ticket-order reading — patterns first, tickets second.
Fix without verify-tomorrow — the loop must close.
Waiting for tickets on correlated signals — the audit escalates directly.
lessons.try_it: Run the 10-minute scan on an invented audit day: list the patterns you'd flag.

lessons.title: The operator's seat in an incident
concepts: When a block becomes an incident, the operator's role shifts: from POLICY decisions to CONTAINMENT support — isolate hosts, pull audit evidence, enforce emergency rules, and feed the IR team. Know your seat before the incident.

Your four incident jobs: ISOLATE (network-quarantine the host via policy — faster than a walk to the desk), EVIDENCE (freeze the audit trail: export the host's deny/allow history before it ages), CONTAIN (emergency rules: block the hash fleet-wide, kill the egress), COMMUNICATE (status to the IR lead, not freelance analysis).

Don't freelance the investigation: the IR team owns the hunt. Your value is speed on the controls and completeness on the evidence — the operator who starts their own forensic adventure slows the response.
Know the escalation path cold: who declares an incident, who you call, what 'isolate' means in your tooling. The incident is not the time to learn the console's quarantine button.

example.code:
INCIDENT SEAT
  isolate:     network-quarantine via policy (fast)
  evidence:    freeze + export the host's audit trail
  contain:     emergency rules (block hash, kill egress)
  communicate: status to IR lead (no freelance hunting)
example.walkthrough: Know your seat before the page: isolate via policy, freeze and export evidence, contain with emergency rules, and brief the IR lead. Speed on the controls, completeness on the evidence, no freelance hunting.

pitfalls: Freelance forensics — the IR team hunts; you enable.
Learning the quarantine button mid-incident — drills exist for this.
Investigating instead of isolating — containment first, curiosity second.
lessons.try_it: Write your incident seat card: the exact console steps for isolate, evidence-freeze, and emergency block.

lessons.title: Containment with endpoint controls
concepts: Network quarantine via policy: cut the host's egress (except to the management plane) in one rule — the host can still report, but can't spread or exfiltrate. Faster and more reliable than pulling cables.
Emergency hash block: the malicious binary's hash denied fleet-wide in minutes — the same allowlist, inverted for the incident. One rule, whole fleet, immediate.
Egress kill for the C2: the destination denied at the firewall layer fleet-wide. Even if the binary runs somewhere unprotected, its phone-home dies.

Containment is reversible by design: quarantine rules are time-boxed and ticketed, with the release criteria written at creation ('release when IR confirms clean'). Containment without a release plan becomes a permanent outage.

example.code:
CONTAINMENT TOOLKIT
  quarantine: host egress cut (mgmt plane excepted)
  hash block: malicious hash denied fleet-wide
  egress kill: C2 destination denied fleet-wide
  every rule: time-boxed + ticketed + release criteria
example.walkthrough: Contain with the toolkit: policy quarantine (management plane excepted), fleet-wide hash block, egress kill on the C2 — every rule time-boxed, ticketed, with release criteria written at creation.

pitfalls: Pulling cables instead of policy quarantine — slower, and kills reporting too.
Containment without release criteria — the quarantine becomes permanent.
Forgetting the management plane exception — the quarantined host must still report.
lessons.try_it: Build the containment toolkit runbook: exact steps for each of the four, with the release criteria template.

lessons.title: Evidence for the IR team
concepts: Freeze first: export the host's full audit history (denies, allows, policy changes, tamper events) before retention or rotation touches it. Evidence frozen in the first hour is evidence; evidence reconstructed later is narrative.

The evidence packet: timeline (first malicious signal → detection → containment), the binaries (hashes, signers, paths), the behaviors (what the audit shows it tried), the scope (which hosts, which users, which data), and the control actions taken (what you isolated/blocked and when).
Chain of custody for the packet: who exported, when, from which system, hash of the export. The IR team (and later, possibly legal) needs to trust the packet — custody is how.
Don't filter for them: export the host's FULL relevant history, not your summary of it. Your triage notes accompany the packet; they don't replace it. The IR team finds things you filtered out.

example.code:
EVIDENCE PACKET
  freeze:  export host audit history (hour one)
  packet:  timeline + binaries + behaviors + scope + actions
  custody:  who/when/source/hash of export
  rule:     full history, not your filtered summary
example.walkthrough: Freeze the host's full audit history in the first hour, packet it as timeline plus binaries plus behaviors plus scope plus actions, and record the chain of custody. Export everything relevant — your notes annotate, never replace.

pitfalls: Filtered exports — your summary replaces their evidence; don't.
Late freezing — retention ate the early signals.
No custody record — the packet's trustworthiness is undocumented.
lessons.try_it: Assemble a practice evidence packet for an invented incident: timeline, binaries, behaviors, scope, actions.

lessons.title: Post-incident: the operations learning loop
concepts: The postmortem asks operations questions: which control detected it (or should have)? What was the time from signal to containment? Did the runbooks work? What does the audit show we missed?

Every incident produces control improvements: the missed detection becomes a rule, the slow containment becomes a runbook fix, the blind spot becomes a monitoring addition. 'No changes needed' is the wrong postmortem conclusion — always.

The operator's postmortem contribution: the timeline of control actions (isolated at X, blocked at Y), the audit evidence that mattered, and the honest assessment of what was slow or confusing. Write it within 48 hours, while the friction is fresh.

Track incident metrics: signal-to-containment time (the number that matters), detection source distribution (which controls catch things?), and repeat-incident rate. The trend is the program's report card.

example.code:
POSTMORTEM (ops section)
  detection: which control? (or which should have?)
  timeline:  signal -> containment (the number)
  runbooks:  what worked / what confused
  improvements: rule + runbook + monitoring (always)
  metrics:   signal-to-containment trend
example.walkthrough: Write the ops postmortem within 48 hours: which control detected, signal-to-containment time, what the runbooks got wrong, and the concrete improvements. Track the trend — it's the program's report card.

pitfalls: 'No changes needed' postmortems — the incident taught nothing.
Late postmortems — friction forgotten is friction repeated.
Blame-focused reviews — the process failed; fix the process.
lessons.try_it: Write the ops section of a postmortem for the Word/PowerShell incident: detection, timeline, improvements.

simulations.title: The incident responder's tool got blocked
simulations.brief: During an active intrusion, the responder's forensic tool was blocked by the allowlist policy on the compromised host. The responder is demanding the policy be disabled. Diagnose before you decide.

steps.symptom: Block event: forensic-tool.exe denied on WS-301 at 14:22. Policy: default-deny. The tool hash is not in the allowlist.
options: Disable the endpoint policy so the responder can work
Verify the tool: check the hash against the vendor's published value, confirm the responder's identity and ticket, then approve the specific hash in a scoped, time-boxed policy exception
Tell the responder to work without the tool
Add *\*.exe to the allowlist temporarily
evidence: block-log.txt
14:22 deny forensic-tool.exe sha256:9f2c... on WS-301. Policy: default-deny, Learning Mode expired 90 days ago.
vendor-hash.txt
Published sha256 for forensic-tool v3.2: 9f2c... — matches the blocked binary. Ticket INC-4412 names this responder and host.
steps.explain: Default-deny did its job — it blocked an unknown binary, even a legitimate one. The answer is never 'turn off the control during the incident'; it is verify the hash, scope the exception to that hash on that host, and time-box it.

steps.symptom: Hash verified, exception granted for 4 hours on WS-301. The responder now asks for a permanent exception 'for next time.' Your call?
options: Make it permanent — responders need their tools
Deny permanent: approve the tool through the normal change process (hash pinned in the gold image policy, change ticket, review) instead of a standing exception
Extend the exception to 30 days
Allowlist the whole tools folder
evidence: change-process.txt
Permanent allowlist entries require: vendor hash verification, change ticket, security review, and inclusion in the baseline policy — not a ticket-time exception.
steps.explain: Temporary exceptions are incident tools; permanent entries are architecture. Routing the tool through the proper change process gets the responder their tool forever, without a standing hole punched in a panic.

simulations.debrief: Allowlisting will block legitimate tools — that is the price of default-deny, and it is worth paying. The discipline: verify the hash, scope the exception, time-box it, and route permanence through change control.

simulations.title: The elevation request at 4:55 PM
simulations.brief: A developer requests local admin elevation to install a driver package, 5 minutes before the change freeze. The package is unsigned. Decide.

steps.symptom: Request: local admin for 2 hours, unsigned driver installer, justification 'need it for tomorrow's demo.' No ticket, no manager approval.
options: Approve — the demo matters
Deny as requested; counter with just-in-time elevation for the signed version through the normal change window, with the installer hash verified and the session recorded
Approve permanently — developers need admin
Ignore the request
evidence: elevation-policy.txt
JIT elevation: time-boxed, recorded, hash-verified, manager-approved, never during freeze without incident ticket. Unsigned drivers: never elevated, no exceptions.
threat-intel.txt
Unsigned 'driver packages' are a top initial-access vector; BYOVD (bring your own vulnerable driver) attacks abuse exactly this path.
steps.explain: Elevation is not a favor — it is a privileged-access decision. Unsigned code plus no ticket plus freeze window is three red flags; the counter-offer (signed, verified, recorded, in-window) meets the real need without the risk.

steps.symptom: The developer returns with a signed installer, a manager-approved ticket, and agrees to the change window tomorrow. Final decision?
options: Still deny — developers should never have admin
Approve JIT elevation: 1 hour, recorded session, hash-pinned installer, auto-revoke — the request now meets every policy condition
Approve for the whole week to be safe
Approve without recording to save time
evidence: ticket.txt
CHG-8821 approved by manager, installer hash pinned, window 09:00–10:00 tomorrow, session recording enabled.
steps.explain: Just-in-time elevation exists precisely for this: legitimate need, bounded blast radius, full accountability. Denying a compliant request teaches people to bypass the process; approving it properly teaches them to use it.

simulations.debrief: Elevation decisions are risk decisions with a paper trail. Deny the non-compliant request, approve the compliant one with bounds and recording — the process must be easier to use than to bypass.

simulations.title: The ringfenced browser tried to escape
simulations.brief: Ringfencing contained it: the browser tried to launch powershell.exe and was denied. But the attempt itself means something got into the browser. Respond.

steps.symptom: Ringfence deny: chrome.exe -> powershell.exe blocked 11:47. Preceding: user opened an invoice attachment from an unknown sender at 11:42.
options: Containment held — close the ticket, the control worked

Containment held AND investigate: the block proves the control works, but the launch attempt proves malicious content reached the browser — isolate the host, analyze the attachment, hunt for what else it tried
Remove the ringfence so the browser works normally
Reinstall Chrome
evidence: ringfence-log.txt
11:47 deny: chrome.exe attempted CreateProcess powershell.exe -enc <blob>. Policy: browsers may not spawn shells. Precedent: none in 90 days.
email.txt
11:42 invoice.doc from unknown sender, macros enabled by user. Attachment hash matches a known Qakbot loader.
steps.explain: Ringfencing is containment, not cure. The deny event is a detection: malicious content executed far enough to try escaping. Celebrate the control, then work the intrusion it revealed.

steps.symptom: Attachment confirmed malicious (Qakbot loader). The browser was ringfenced, but what else must you verify?
options: Nothing — the ringfence stopped it

Verify the full kill chain was contained: check for persistence mechanisms, credential access attempts, and lateral movement from this host — ringfencing blocks categories of behavior, and you must confirm nothing else slipped a different path
Delete the email
Block the sender domain and move on
evidence: hunt.txt
Host EDR: no persistence created, no lateral movement, but 3 credential-dump attempts (all denied by a second policy). The loader tried 4 techniques; 1 was attempted, 3 were pre-blocked.
steps.explain: Assume-breach thinking: the control stopped what it saw, but the attacker tried four things. Verify each one failed — the hunt is not over until every attempted technique is accounted for.

simulations.debrief: Ringfencing turns 'the browser got exploited' from a disaster into a detection. The control contains; the analyst still hunts. Every blocked escape attempt is an incident until proven otherwise.

simulations.title: The blocked USB at the finance desk
simulations.brief: Storage Control blocked a USB write on a finance workstation: 2.1 GB attempted to an unapproved device. The user says it was 'just a backup.' Respond.

steps.symptom: Block event: 2.1 GB write to unapproved USB on FIN-04, user k.osei, 16:40. File types: .xlsx, .pdf — names match payroll directories.
options: Approve the device — the user explained it
Treat as potential exfiltration until assessed: isolate the data question first — what was being copied, is it sensitive, was there authorization — while preserving the block
Confiscate the USB immediately
Disable Storage Control for finance
evidence: dlp-log.txt
File names: payroll-q3.xlsx, bonuses-2026.pdf. Classification: confidential. No approved removable-media request on file for k.osei.
policy.txt
Storage Control: unapproved devices blocked by default. Assessment before accusation: determine data, authorization, and intent through proper channels.
steps.explain: The control worked — the data did not leave. Now assess like an investigator, not a prosecutor: what data, what authorization, what intent. The block gives you time to ask; use it.

steps.symptom: Assessment: k.osei was taking payroll files home to 'work over the weekend.' No malicious intent found, but a clear policy violation with confidential data. Disposition?
options: Fire the user
Document the violation, require secure remote-access training, provide an approved encrypted transfer method for legitimate after-hours work, and keep the block in place
Do nothing — no harm done
Approve all USB devices to avoid friction
evidence: hr-note.txt
First violation, 6-year clean record, cooperative. Remediation: training + approved workflow. Repeat violations escalate per policy.
steps.explain: Security that only punishes teaches concealment. The fix addresses the real problem — the user had no approved way to work after hours — while keeping the control and documenting the lesson.

simulations.debrief: Storage Control turns exfiltration attempts into teachable moments. Block first, assess fairly, fix the workflow gap — controls plus usable alternatives beat controls plus resentment.

simulations.title: Emergency policy change outside the window
simulations.brief: A critical app breaks at 8 PM due to a policy misconfiguration. The fix is a one-line allowlist change, but the change window is tomorrow at 6 AM and the app supports the night shift. Decide.

steps.symptom: Broken: night-shift logistics app, 40 users idle. Fix: allowlist one verified hash. Risk of the change: minimal (single hash, tested in staging). Risk of waiting: 10 hours of downtime.
options: Wait for the window — process is process
Emergency change: apply the fix now with documented emergency approval, peer review of the hash, automatic rollback plan, and retroactive change-ticket review tomorrow
Apply the fix quietly and tell no one
Disable the endpoint policy until morning
evidence: emergency-process.txt
Emergency changes permitted when: business impact is severe, the change is minimal and reversible, two-person approval is obtained, and a rollback plan exists. Full review within 24h.
hash-verify.txt
Hash verified against vendor + staging test passed. Reversal: single rule deletion, <2 min.
steps.explain: Change control exists to manage risk, not to worship the calendar. The emergency path — bounded change, two-person rule, rollback plan, retroactive review — is the process working as designed under pressure.

steps.symptom: Emergency change applied, app restored. What happens tomorrow?
options: Nothing — it worked
Retroactive review: the change ticket is completed with evidence, the emergency justification is recorded, and the incident feeds the policy QA process so the misconfiguration does not recur
Revert the change to follow the window
Delete the emergency approval record
evidence: qa-note.txt
Root cause: hash changed in vendor update, policy not refreshed. Fix: add vendor-update monitoring to policy QA checklist.
steps.explain: The emergency path is a loan, not a gift — it gets repaid with documentation and a root-cause fix. Otherwise every change becomes an 'emergency' and change control is dead.

simulations.debrief: Change control must bend without breaking. Emergency paths with approval, reversibility, and retroactive review keep the business running and the audit trail intact.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.

Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before

Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened

Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.

ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
media.alt: 24-hour timeline showing a shaded normal login window from 8 AM to 6 PM with normal logins inside it, and a red anomaly marker at 2:47 AM for a foreign login scoring 97 out of 100.

media.title: Indirect prompt injection attack flow
media.caption: An attacker hides instructions in data the agent retrieves; the agent mistakes data for instructions and misuses its tools.
media.alt: Attack flow diagram: hidden instruction in an email is read by an AI agent, which mistakes it for a command and calls a privileged tool, causing fraud; three defense boxes below: sanitize content, least-privilege tools, human approval.
